Right-click a sheet in the Project Index ➤ Rename… to change its number and name in Sheet Title. The other parameters of the sheet are in the element panel: Sheet Number, Sheet Name, Sheet Issue Date, Drawn By, Checked By, Designed By, Approved By, Appears In Sheet List, its guide grid and its revisions. Several sheets picked together in the Project Index (with Ctrl or Shift) are changed together: the panel shows the values they share.

Settings ➤ Settings ➤ Project information sets what every sheet shows: Project Issue Date, Project Status, Client Name, Project Address, Project Name and Project Number.

Views ➤ Create ➤ Schedules ➤ Note Block makes a schedule of the symbols placed with Symbol, of one family only (north arrows, targets, revision deltas…): in New Note Block choose the Family and type the Note Block Name, then OK. Note Block Properties opens first, with the same tabs as any schedule; by default each row shows the symbol's type, its text and the count.

docs.title: Title blocks
docs.text:
The title block shows the project's information, the sheet's number and name, the people and the dates, the current revision and the scale (As indicated when the views have different scales); above it, a table lists the sheet's revisions with their number, description and date. A double click on one of its fields types the value in place.

  • Click a line of the title block to pick it: the type selector changes it to another paper size, Del removes it (the sheet and its views stay).
  • Document ➤ Sheets ➤ Title Block inserts one on the open sheet: choose it in the type selector, its frame follows the cursor, click to place it.
  • Type Parameters shows its Sheet width and Sheet height; Duplicate… makes a new paper size.

docs.title: Views on sheets
docs.text:
Drag a view from the Project Index onto the sheet, or use Document ➤ Sheets ➤ View (Views, then Add View to Sheet): the view follows the cursor at its scale, and a click places it as a viewport. A view goes on one sheet only; a schedule on several.

A picked viewport:

  • moves with the mouse or the arrow keys, unless it is pinned (Fix); near another view, its title lines up with the other's and a dashed line shows it;
  • has its View Scale, its Title on Sheet (also typed by double-clicking the title) and its Rotation on Sheet (90° clockwise or counter-clockwise; the title stays horizontal);
  • shows the end of its title line, which can be dragged;
  • takes a viewport type from the type selector: No Title, Title w/ Line or Title w/o Line, or a type of your own (Show Title, Show Extension Line, line weight, colour and pattern of the line);
  • leaves the sheet with Del; the view stays in the project.
A viewport picked on a sheet

Activate View (on the Selection: Viewports card or the right button) edits the view where it is on the sheet, the rest of the sheet in halftone; Deactivate View goes back to the sheet. A view turned on its sheet cannot be activated: take its rotation off first. A double click on a view opens it in its own window.

Each view on a sheet has a Detail Number: the first number free on that sheet (1, 2, 3…), shown in a circle left of its title. Change it in the viewport's Properties; a number already used on the same sheet is refused. The view's own Properties show where it is placed, read only: Referencing Sheet and Referencing Detail.

docs.title: Text, lines and dimensions on a sheet
docs.text: With a sheet open, Text, Detail line and the dimensions work on the sheet itself: what is drawn there belongs to the sheet, keeps its printed size and is printed with it. Dimensions measure the lines drawn on the sheet. The other tools still open Go to View.

docs.title: Guide grids
docs.text: Document ➤ Sheets ➤ Guide Grid asks for a name and covers the sheet with a grid. Pick it to drag its corners or to set its Guide spacing; the sheet's Guide Grid parameter shows the same grid on other sheets, or none. Views dragged near the grid's lines snap onto them. The grid is never printed.

docs.title: Sheet list
docs.text: Views ➤ Create ➤ Schedules ➤ Sheet List makes a schedule of the sheets: number, name and any other field. Sheets with Appears In Sheet List unticked are left out. Rows ➤ New adds a placeholder sheet: a row that is not a sheet yet and is not in the Project Index. Filter placeholder sheets shows every row, hides the placeholders or shows only them. A placeholder chosen in New Sheet becomes a real sheet.

docs.title: Revisions
docs.text:
Document ➤ Sheets ➤ Sheet Issues/Revisions lists the revisions of the project, one per row: Sequence, Numbering (Numeric, Alphabetic or none), Date, Description, Issued, Issued to, Issued by and Show. Add adds one; a row picked by its sequence number is merged into the one above or below (its clouds go with it) or moved up and down. Numbering is Per Project or Per Sheet (the place of the revision among the sheet's revisions); Alphabetical order ➤ Options… sets the letters used. An issued revision cannot be changed, and neither can its clouds, until Issued is unticked.

Document ➤ Detail ➤ Revision Cloud draws a cloud in a plan, a section, a free 2D view or on a sheet: sketch closed loops with the shapes of the Draw group, then Finish Edit Mode; a selected cloud's Edit Sketch opens them again, unless its revision is issued. The cloud takes the latest revision not issued; picked, it shows its Revision (to change), its number, date and people, its Mark and Comments. Show of a revision draws its clouds and tags, keeps them but does not draw them, or hides them.

A sheet lists the revisions of the clouds of its views and of its own clouds. Its Revisions on Sheet (in the element panel, Edit…) adds other revisions to the list.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
A schedule is a table of the elements of the model, and a view like the others: it opens in a window of the drawing area, is tiled, cascaded and switched with plans, sections and 3D views, and is listed under Schedules/Quantities in the Project Index. It follows every change of the model at once, and every change made in it changes the model.

Schedules beside the plan, selected together

docs.title: Creating a schedule
docs.text: Views ➤ Create ➤ Schedules ➤ Schedule/Quantities opens New Schedule: choose a category, a name (the default follows the category until one is typed) and Schedule building components or Schedule keys. OK opens Schedule Properties; its second OK creates the schedule and opens its view. Material Takeoff in the same menu lists the materials of the layers of walls, floors and roofs.

docs.title: Schedule Properties
docs.text:
The dialog opens again from the element panel of the schedule (each tab has its Edit… button) or from the right button on the schedule in the Project Index. Its tabs:

Tab What it sets Fields The columns, chosen from Available fields: and put in order; the fields of the rooms the elements are in; Add Parameter… for a project or shared parameter; Calculated Value… for a formula (with + - * / ^, sqrt, round, IF, AND, OR, NOT and units) or a percentage Filter Up to four criteria, all of which an element must meet Sorting/Grouping Up to four sort levels, each with Header, footer and Blank line; the grand totals; Itemize every instance (off: one row per type) Formatting Per field: heading, orientation, alignment, hidden field, Format… (units, rounding, symbol), totals and Conditional Format… (a background colour where a value meets a test) Appearance Grid lines and outline with their line styles, the title and the column headers, a blank row, Header text and Body text (size, Bold, Italic); shown when the schedule is on a sheet

docs.title: Working in a schedule view
docs.text:
• A cell edits the element, or its type for a type parameter; every edit is one step of undo.
  • A type parameter (a door's width, a component's depth) changes every instance of the type: Edit Type says how many and asks first.
  • The predefined schedules of the Project Index (doors, floors, rooms, stairs, curtain panels…) work the same way: the type and the level are picked from a list, the values the model computes (areas, volumes, the host wall) are read-only, and in the curtain panel and mullion schedules the type of each panel or inner mullion is picked.
  • A row selects its elements in every view. Highlight in model on the Edit | Schedule/Quantities card opens Show Elements in View, which brings a plan forward framed on them; Show goes on to the next view.
  • Rows ➤ Delete deletes the elements of the selected rows, after asking.
  • Headings picked together are joined under a common heading with Group, and parted with Ungroup; Hide column and Unhide all columns work on the column picked.

docs.title: Schedules on sheets
docs.text:
Drag a schedule from the Project Index onto a sheet. Selected on the sheet, it shows its controls: the Z on the right edge of a segment splits it in two, the arrow in the middle of a segment moves it (dropped on the segment beside it, the two join), the dot at the bottom of a segment moves its last row, and the triangles at the top of the columns set their widths. A double click, or Edit Schedule on the right button, opens the schedule view. The same schedule can go on several sheets.

A schedule on a sheet, with its controls

docs.title: Graphic schedule by type
docs.text:
In View › Create › Schedules › Schedule/Quantities choose Graphic schedule by type and the category: Doors, Windows, Curtain walls or Openings (all three). The schedule has one entry per type, with the type's elevation drawn and dimensioned from the model and its data below; curtain walls have one entry per type and size. With Number missing type marks types without a mark get F1, F2, P1, FC1…, written into the type.

Graphic schedule by type

In Schedule Properties the Layout tab chooses between Table, In columns (one column per type, quantity per level and total), As cards (cards side by side with the area colour, quantity and a Notes row) and Elevations by level (the types of each level on the ground line, with a label and dimensions between types). Type drawing sets front or back view, scale, detail level, width, height and sill dimensions, swing symbol and ground line. Areas and colours splits the schedule into areas with a condition and a colour; Coloured opening tag in plans uses the same colours in plans. Thermal transmittance U and Acoustic class are type fields you fill in. A double click on an entry opens the type's properties. On a sheet the schedule splits like the others.

Graphic schedule by element has one column per door or window (or one row, with a Normal table): a computed classification code (Window - 003), the rooms on both sides, sizes, orientation, sill and head height. In the Fields tab the 2D symbol, Back view and Type elevation (dimensioned) fields draw the model in the cell; for the selected field you set scale, detail level and row height. In Layout you choose the level and whether curtain wall panels are included.

docs.title: Key schedules and material takeoffs
docs.text:
A key schedule (Schedule keys in New Schedule) defines named sets of values, one row per key, added and deleted with Rows. Its Key Name becomes a parameter of the category: choosing a key for an element gives it all the values of that row.

A material takeoff lists, for each element, the materials of its layers with their area and volume; its fields can be sorted, grouped and totalled like any other.

docs.title: Project and shared parameters
docs.text:
Settings ➤ Settings ➤ Project Parameters adds parameters to the elements of some categories, or to their types, with a name, a type of value and the group they show in the element panel.

Settings ➤ Settings ➤ Shared Parameters opens Edit Shared Parameters: the shared parameter file in use (Browse…, Create…), its groups and the parameters of each group. A shared parameter keeps its name and type, and has an identifier of its own, so that several projects add the same parameter. In Parameter Properties, choose Shared parameter and Select… to add one to the project; Export… writes a shared parameter of the project back to the file.

docs.title: Exporting and reusing schedules
docs.text:
• File ➤ Export ➤ Schedule… writes the schedule as delimited text: Export Schedule sets the field delimiter, the text qualifier and which headings and group rows go in the file.
  • Create view template from view… on the right button of a schedule makes a view template with its fields, filter, sorting, formatting and appearance; Apply view template… gives them to another schedule.
  • Save to New File… on the right button writes the schedule's setup, without the elements, to a file of its own. Create ➤ Load from library ➤ Insert from File ➤ Insert Views from File… brings the schedules of another project into this one, with their project parameters.

docs.title: Printing
docs.text: Printing writes PDF files: on the desktop they are saved where you choose, in the browser they are downloaded.

docs.title: The Print dialog
docs.text:
Ctrl+P, or File ➤ Print ➤ Print…, opens Print:

  • File: the name of the file and, when several views or sheets are printed, Combine multiple selected views/sheets into a single file (one page each) or Create separate files (one file each, named after the sheet or view).
  • Print Range: Current window, Visible portion of current window (only what the window shows), or Selected views/sheets with Select….
  • Reverse print order prints the last page first.
  • Settings: the print settings in use, changed with Settings…; Preview shows the pages.
Print

Plans, sections, elevations, free 2D views and sheets print as drawings; the 3D window prints as an image of the view; a schedule prints its table on a page. The page is always white, elements hidden temporarily in a window are printed, and each printed sheet carries the date and time of the print.

docs.title: View/sheet sets
docs.text: Select… opens View/Sheet Set: tick the sheets and views to print (Show sheets, views or both; Check all, Check none). A set is saved by name with Save As… and kept in the project; Save, Reset, Rename… and Delete manage the saved sets, and the name list picks one again.

docs.title: Print Setup
docs.text:
File ➤ Print ➤ Print Setup…, or Settings… in Print, sets:

Setting What it does Size and Orientation The paper (A0 to A4, or the sheet's own size) and its orientation Paper Placement Center, or an offset from the lower-left corner Hidden line views Vector Processing (sections and elevations print only the lines that are seen: the lines behind nearer surfaces are removed, not just covered, and lines lying on one another print once, so the PDF opens clean in other programs) or Raster Processing (the pages as images, at the raster quality chosen) Zoom Fit to page, or a percentage of the real size Colors Black Lines, Grayscale or Colour Options Show view links in blue, Hide unreferenced view tags, Hide crop boundaries, Replace halftone with thin lines, Keep coincident lines (off: two lines lying on one another in printed and exported sections and elevations become one; on: both stay, each with its own element) Print Setup

Settings are saved by name with Save As…, and kept in the project. Closing the dialog after changing saved settings asks whether to save the changes; No keeps them for this session only.

docs.title: Print Preview
docs.text: File ➤ Print ➤ Print Preview, or Preview in Print, shows the pages as they will print, in their colours: Previous Page and Next Page go through them, the wheel zooms and dragging pans; Print… prints, Close goes back.

docs.title: Exporting images
docs.text:
File ➤ Export ➤ Image… opens Export Image:

  • the file name and the Export Range: the current window, its visible portion, or the views and sheets chosen (one file each);
  • the Image Size: Fit view(s)/sheet(s) to a number of pixels across or down, or a zoom percentage of the real size at a resolution;
  • the options, as for printing: view links in blue, crop boundaries and unreferenced view tags hidden;
  • the Format of views without shading and of shaded views: PNG, JPEG, BMP or TIFF.

The 3D window is exported as it is shown, with its graphic style.

docs.title: Floors, roofs, stairs and components
docs.text: Floors, roofs, stairs and railings are drawn in sketch mode: their lines are sketched first, and the element is made only when the sketch is finished. Components (furniture, casework and plumbing fixtures) are placed with a click. Curtain walls are described in Walls, doors and windows.

docs.title: Sketch mode
docs.text:
Create ▸ Build ▸ Flooring, Roof, Stairs and Railing open sketch mode. The contextual card is named after what is sketched (Edit | Create Floor Boundary, Create Roof Footprint, Create Stairs Sketch, Create Railing Path) and has:

  • the Mode group: Finish Edit Mode makes the element; Cancel Edit Mode drops the sketch and leaves the model as it was;
  • the Draw group, with the drawing tools of the element;
  • for stairs and railings, the Tools group.
Sketch mode: the contextual card and the magenta lines

Nothing is made while sketching: the lines are magenta, and the model changes only with Finish Edit Mode. The whole element is then one step of the undo history: one Ctrl+Z takes it away.

docs.title: Drawing lines
docs.text:
Tool How it draws Line Click point after point: each click ends a line and starts the next. The length and angle of the line under the cursor are shown beside it; Shift keeps it horizontal or vertical. With Continue off on the options strip, each line is drawn on its own. Clicking the start of the chain again closes the loop Type a length and press Enter: the line ends that far along the cursor's direction (a stair's run too). Rectangle Two opposite corners: four lines Pick Walls Click a wall: its line is added to the sketch (see below). Press Tab over a wall, then click, to pick the whole chain of walls joined end to end Pick Lines Move over a wall, a grid, a line or the edge of a floor or roof: the line under the cursor is highlighted and named (a wall's faces, each layer boundary, its two Core Boundary lines and its axis); Tab goes to the next one there. Click to add a sketch line on it (set off by Offset towards the cursor) Slope Arrow Click the tail, then the head of the arrow (floors and roofs)

Offset on the options strip moves the drawn lines (and the lines of picked walls) by that distance.

The arcs of the Draw group (and a circle, as two halves) are one sketch line each: picked, measured and dragged as arcs, kept by the floor, roof, stair, wall boundary or filled region, and given back as arcs by Edit Boundary or Edit Sketch. In every view a sketch point snaps to the ends and middles of the sketch's lines and arcs, to arcs' centres, where lines cross and onto a line or an arc; from the point being drawn from, to the foot of a perpendicular and to the point where a line touches an arc. The marker and its name show where the point snaps; S C and S P ask for the centre or the perpendicular for the next point.

Floors and roofs need closed loops. A loop drawn inside the outer one is an opening: the floor or the roof has a hole there. When Finish Edit Mode finds lines that do not close or that cross, a message says so and the sketch stays open to be fixed (Continue).

docs.title: Picking and changing sketch lines
docs.text:
Esc ends the chain being drawn; a second Esc puts the drawing tool down (so does Modify). While the sketch is open its lines are elements of the view, and Modify works on them as on other lines; nothing else can be picked until the sketch is finished:

  • the line under the cursor is highlighted; a click selects it, Ctrl adds lines, Shift takes them away, a window selects several, Tab the chain of joined lines;
  • the end of a line selected on its own drags alone: the line next to it stays where it is and the join is broken; with a chain selected (Tab), the ends where its lines meet drag together; a dragged line takes the lines joined to it along;
  • Move, Copy, Rotate, Mirror on Line, Repeat in Series, Align, Offset, Shorten/Lengthen and Split Element work on them, and the sketch stays open;
  • one selected line shows temporary dimensions to the nearest parallel line on each side (another sketch line, the wall's original outline, a wall, a grid, a level): click the value and type a distance to move the line; the symbol beside it makes a permanent dimension, kept while the sketch is open;
  • its properties are in the element panel: Defines Slope and Slope, for a roof line picked from a wall its Overhang, and its Length.

Align takes as its reference the line under the cursor, and Tab goes to the next one there, so a sketch line can be aligned to a wall's layer or core boundary. While drawing or dragging an end, the points snap to the corners of the walls' faces, layers and core boundaries, then onto those lines. Del deletes the selected lines. Ctrl+Z while sketching takes back the last change to the sketch, not to the model. All this works in plans, in sections and elevations (a wall's boundary) and, for selecting, dragging ends and deleting, in the 3D view.

docs.title: Editing the sketch of an element
docs.text:
Select a floor, a roof, a stair or a railing: the Mode group of its contextual card has Edit Boundary (floors), Edit Footprint (roofs), Edit Sketch (stairs) or Edit Path (railings). Sketch mode opens with the element's lines, openings, slopes and arrow; Finish Edit Mode changes the same element, Cancel Edit Mode leaves it unchanged.

The sketch opens with Modify active: its lines can be selected and changed at once.

In a plan the sketch is drawn on the level; in the 3D view it lies on the element's own plane (the floor's top, the roof's base) and the 3D view stays open.

A new floor can be sketched in the 3D view too: Flooring started there puts the sketch on the plane of the level, the line being drawn follows the cursor with its length, and Finish Edit Mode makes the floor without leaving the 3D view. In the 3D view the options strip's Level chooses the work plane: the level whose plane the sketch lies on and the floor goes on. Pick Walls takes the wall whose face is under the cursor. Roofs by footprint, stairs and railings are sketched in a plan.

docs.title: Floors
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Flooring. Sketch mode starts with Pick Walls.
  2. Click the walls around the floor, or press Tab over one of them and click to pick them all. Each line goes on the interior face of its wall; the lines of walls that meet are trimmed or extended to meet at the corner.
  3. Or draw the boundary with Line or Rectangle; draw a loop inside it for an opening.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.
A floor: TAB on the walls, click, Finish Edit Mode

On the options strip, Extend into wall (to core) puts picked lines into the wall up to the face of its core, and Offset moves them (a negative offset moves them away from the walls). The type of the new floor is the one in the type selector at the top of Properties.

docs.title: Sloped floors
docs.text:
A floor slopes in one direction, set in one of two ways while sketching:

  • a Slope Arrow: its properties are Specify (Height at Tail, from the heights of its two ends, or Slope), Height Offset at Tail, Height Offset at Head and Slope. The heights are measured from the top of the floor;
  • one boundary line with Defines Slope ticked and its Slope in degrees: the floor rises from that line, inwards.

The floor is sloped in 3D and in sections. Its Slope Angle in Properties changes the slope afterwards.

docs.title: Floors over walls
docs.text: When a floor crosses walls (an upper floor resting on the walls below, for instance), its slab is cut out of them: in 3D and in sections the wall stops under the floor and goes on above it, and walls go on through the floor's openings.

docs.title: Floor properties
docs.text:
Property What it is Level, Height Offset From Level The level and the height of the top face from it Slope Angle The slope of a sloped floor, in degrees Thickness From the type's layers (read-only) Perimeter, Area, Volume Without the openings (read-only) Comments, Mark Free text The properties of a floor

Type Parameters has the floor's Structure (its layers) and its default thickness.

docs.title: Roofs
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Roof. Sketch mode starts with Pick Walls; the options strip has Defines Slope, Overhang and Extend into wall (to core).
  2. Pick the walls (Tab for the whole chain). Each line goes on the exterior face of its wall, moved out by the overhang (from the face of the core with Extend into wall (to core)).
  3. Or draw the footprint with Line or Rectangle; a loop inside is an opening.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.
A roof: the footprint, then the roof

Every line with Defines Slope rises inwards at its Slope (30° by default); a small triangle with the slope is drawn beside it. The shape comes from those lines:

  • all the lines define the slope: a hip roof;
  • two opposite lines do not: a gable roof, the walls under the gables rise to the ridge when attached;
  • no line defines the slope: a flat roof, or a roof sloping along a Slope Arrow (then no line may define a slope).
Hip, gable and flat

To change one line, press Esc twice, click the line and change Defines Roof Slope, Slope or (lines picked from walls) Overhang in Properties.

Select walls, click Modify Wall ▸ Link Top/Base, then the roof: they rise to its underside, gables included (Walls, doors and windows tells more).

docs.title: Roof properties
docs.text:
Property What it is Base Level, Base Offset From Level Where the eaves are: by default on top of the walls of the level Slope The slope of every line that defines one (or of the arrow) Thickness, Maximum Ridge Height, Area, Volume Read-only Comments, Mark Free text

In plan a roof shows its outline, ridges and hips; in 3D its slopes, overhangs and layers.

docs.title: Extrusion roofs
docs.text:
An extrusion roof is an open profile drawn on a vertical work plane and pushed along the plane's normal: a canopy over a door, a barrel roof, a dormer roof drawn on the front wall.

  1. Open an elevation, a section or a 3D view (started in a plan, Go to View asks for one).
  2. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Roof ▾ ▸ Extruded roof. The Work Plane dialog opens: pick a named plane, or Pick a plane and click a wall's face, a grid or a reference plane. The plane must be vertical.
  3. In Roof Reference Level and Offset choose the Level (the highest one by default) and the Offset: a dashed line marks that height.
  4. Draw the profile as one open chain with Line, the arcs or Pick Lines. It is the roof's top: the layers of the roof type hang under it.
  5. Click Finish Edit Mode. The roof runs from the plane (Extrusion Start 0) across the building, away from you (Extrusion End).

A closed profile, a branch or a profile that turns back over itself (a part over another, or a vertical line) is refused at Finish Edit Mode with the reason: an extruded roof must face up.

Selected, an extrusion roof has Edit profile (in an elevation or section facing its plane, or in 3D) and Edit Work Plane; in a plan and in 3D the arrows at its two ends drag Extrusion Start and Extrusion End. Walls attach to its underside as to any roof, and Opening ▸ Vertical cuts it. It follows its plane: when the wall it was drawn on moves, the roof moves with it.

Property What it is Work Plane The plane of the profile (read-only; change it with Edit Work Plane) Extrusion Start, Extrusion End Where the extrusion begins and ends, along the plane's normal Reference level, Level Offset The height the profile is measured from: the whole roof moves with them Rafter Cut, Fascia Depth How the eaves at the two ends of the profile are cut Thickness, Area, Volume Read-only

docs.title: Joining roofs
docs.text:
Modify ▸ Shapes ▸ Join roof (in the BIMopen style Modify ▸ Join roof) joins a roof to another roof's top face or to a wall: the dormer's roof meets the main roof.

  1. Click Join roof. The roof edges highlight under the cursor, in a plan, a section, an elevation or a 3D view.
  2. Click the edge to join: an edge that does not define the slope (a gable), or an end of an extrusion roof.
  3. Click the roof or the wall to join it to. The edge moves out (or back) until the roof meets the other roof's top face, or the wall's face; what lies under that face is cut away.

A joined edge shows orange: clicking it again disjoins it. The join follows: when the main roof's slope or height changes the joined roof meets it again, and a join to a deleted roof goes.

docs.title: Sloped glazing
docs.text:
A sloped glazing is a roof made of glass: a footprint or an extrusion roof whose type is Sloped Glazing. Every planar face of the roof carries curtain grids, mullions and panels.

  1. Draw the roof as usual (Roof or Extruded roof).
  2. Select it and pick Sloped Glazing in the type selector. The first time, BIMopen makes the type with the project's glazed panel and mullions.
  3. Each face is divided by the type's two grids: grid 1 runs up the slope, spaced along the eaves; grid 2 runs along the eaves, spaced up the slope.

With the glazing selected, the curtain tools work on the face under the cursor, in a plan, a section, an elevation or a 3D view:

  • Curtain grid places a line where you click: of grid 1 near the eaves or the ridge, of grid 2 near a side. Press TAB to switch to the other grid. All Segments, One Segment and All Except Picked work as on a curtain wall.
  • Mullion puts mullions of the chosen type on a Grid Line, a Grid Line Segment or All Grid Lines of the face.
  • Panel changes the panel you click to the type in the selector: glazed, solid, a door or empty.
  • Add/Remove Segments takes off the segment you click (the two panels become one), or puts it back.
Property What it is Curtain Panel (type) The panel of every cell Join Condition (type) Which mullions run through where the grids cross: grid 1, grid 2, or the borders with one of them Grid 1/2 Pattern (type): Layout, Spacing, Adjust for Mullion Size How each grid places its lines: none, a fixed distance, a fixed number, a maximum spacing Grid 1/2 Mullions (type): Interior Type, Border 1 Type, Border 2 Type The mullions on the lines and on the face's edges Number, Justification, Angle, Offset of grid 1 and 2 This roof's own values: how many lines (a fixed number), where the remainder goes, how the lines turn on the face (−89° to 89°), how far they move Panels, Mullions Read-only counts

In a plan the glazing shows its panels and mullions seen from above; Visibility/Graphics hides curtain panels and mullions as for curtain walls. IFC writes a roof made of plates and members.

docs.title: Soffits
docs.text:
A soffit closes the underside of the eaves, between the walls and the roof's edge.

  1. In a plan or a 3D view click Create ▸ Build ▸ Roof ▾ ▸ Soffit. Sketch mode starts with Pick Roof Edges.
  2. Click the roof's edges: their lines stay locked to the roof.
  3. Click Pick Walls and the exterior faces of the walls under the roof (TAB picks the chain): these lines stay locked to the walls.
  4. Close the outline with Line and Shorten/Lengthen, then click Finish Edit Mode.

The soffit's top is under the roof's eaves; its layers (the type's Structure) hang below. When the roof or the walls move, the soffit follows them. A Slope Arrow, or a line that Defines Slope, slopes it. Selected, Edit Boundary opens its sketch again.

Property What it is Structure, Thickness (type) The layers, top down, and their sum Level, Height Offset From Level Where its top is Room Bounding Whether rooms stop at it Slope Replaces the slope of its sloping line or arrow Perimeter, Area, Volume Read-only

Sections cut it with its layers, the ceiling plan of its level sees it from below; it has its own category in Visibility/Graphics and in schedules, and IFC writes it as a covering.

docs.title: Stairs
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Vertical Links ▸ Stairs. Sketch mode starts with Run.
  2. Click where the first riser is, then where the run ends: the run snaps to whole treads, and the status bar counts the risers made and left (for example 9 risers created, 8 remaining).
  3. To turn, click again away from the end of the first run and draw the next one: a landing joins them. At any angle the landing is bounded by the two runs' risers, its outer corner where their outer sides meet; where the runs end out of line their inner sides also run on until they meet, a square corner rather than a slanting edge.
  4. When every riser is placed, click Finish Edit Mode.
A stair by runs: the count of risers made and left

Dashed guides show where the next run can start: the last run's extension beyond its end and the lines of its first and last risers. A click near them snaps onto them. In a 3D view the stair is drawn the same way, on the plane of the active level.

A curved run (a spiral stair): with Run active, click Center-ends arc, then the centre, the start of the run line (its distance from the centre is the radius of the walking line) and the end, going round past half a turn if needed, but under one turn (further, the run stops short and the status bar warns that the runs would overlap). The risers radiate from the centre a tread apart on the run line; riser lines drawn radiating from a centre make a curved run too. A second curved run round the same centre and on the same run line (a click near them takes them) is joined to the first by a landing along the arc.

A stair can also be drawn by its lines. In its sketch, click Draw ▸ Boundary and draw the left and right edges (green), then Riser and draw the riser lines (black) between them, with Line or Pick Lines. Parallel, evenly spaced risers make a run, as wide as the risers; a landing joins two runs out to the boundary lines. Each riser is as high as the storey divided by the desired number of risers; with fewer riser lines the stair stops short of the top (Properties shows the actual number). Edit Sketch gives the same lines back. Each run drawn with Run is at once boundary and riser lines like these: they can be moved or deleted like the others. A landing follows its boundary lines: split its far edge with Split Element and drag a piece to notch it, or draw it wider than the runs.

Riser lines need not be straight or parallel: draw them with any drawing tool, an arc too, or slant one. Each tread is then the area between a riser line and the next one of its run, bounded by the boundary lines, and the landing the area between the last riser of one run and the first of the next; the stair is built that way in plan, section, elevation and 3D (a monolithic stair as one slab under its treads), and its railings follow the boundary lines over those treads. A riser line running past a boundary is cut there. A riser line that does not touch both boundaries, or more or fewer riser lines than the stair's height needs, gives a warning; the stair is made all the same. A stair drawn this way keeps its lines when Width or Actual Tread Depth changes: change them in Edit Sketch. The risers follow one another as the boundaries join them, whichever line was drawn first: the stair starts at the riser the first boundary line starts on, otherwise at the first riser drawn; a tread drawn deeper than the others (short of a landing) stays in its run. The type's Nosing Length and Nosing Profile run along each riser line, and along the edge of a landing over the riser that reaches it (in plan, a line in front of each riser); its Middle Stringers run under the treads from riser line to riser line, following them where the boundaries turn; a monolithic stair's Underside of Stringer is Smooth or Stepped here too.

The Width on the options strip is that of the new stair (by default the type's). Tools ▸ Railing Type chooses the railings of the new stair: a railing type, put on both sides, or None.

The number of risers comes from the height between Base Level and Top Level (with their offsets) and the type's Maximum Riser Height; changing a level or an offset in Properties changes the risers. Edit Sketch reopens its boundary and riser lines: change or delete them (click, Del) and draw runs again; the railings of the stair follow. Multistory Top Level repeats the stair, with its railings, storey by storey up to that level; a storey whose height is not the stair's gets no copy, and a warning names it. With the stair selected, the blue flip arrows beside its first riser make it go up from the other end; Up Label, Up Arrow, Down Label and Down Arrow in Properties show or hide the plan symbol's parts. The square grip under the UP text drags it elsewhere.

In the plan of its base level the stair shows its treads up to the cut line, the break line, the arrow and the UP text; in the plan of its top level it shows all of it, landings and railings included, with no break line, and the arrow and the DN text down to the first riser. On a level between two storeys of a multistory stair both parts show; in 3D its treads and risers, or a monolithic slab, its landings and railings.

A stair in plan

On the base level the part of the stair above the cut is drawn too, dashed. Each part has a subcategory of Stairs in Styles by Category: Outlines, Riser Lines, Nosing Lines, Supports, Cut Marks and Up Arrows, each also ; their weight, colour and pattern change there, and view by view in Visibility and Graphics.

Annotations ▸ Tag ▸ Tread Number: choose the Reference (Left, Left Quarter, Center, Right Quarter, Right), what to number (Risers or Treads) and the Start Number in the options bar, then click a stair in a plan. Its steps are numbered one after the other through all its runs, in that plan only. With the stair selected, its Properties show the numbering's settings.

docs.title: How a stair is built
docs.text:
Type Parameters of the stair decide its construction:

  • Monolithic Stairs ticked: each run is a concrete slab cut to the steps; its underside runs parallel to the slope, Structural Depth below the inner corners of the steps, and the landings are as thick: the sloping underside of a run meets the landing's underside along a line, without a step; each run ends with its last tread: the landing, flush with it, or the floor above makes the last riser, so steps and slab show as one solid with no line across the risers.
  • otherwise treads (Tread Thickness) with risers (Riser Type Straight, Riser Thickness) or open (None), on stringers: Right Stringer and Left Stringer Closed (a board the treads are housed in), Open (a board cut to the steps, the treads on top) or None, and Middle Stringers under the treads, with their Stringer Thickness and Stringer Height.
  • Begin with Riser and End with Riser cleared: the board of the stair's first or last riser is not built.
  • Riser Type Slanted leans each riser board, its top under the front of the tread above; Riser to Tread Connection runs each tread under the riser behind it (Extend Tread Under Riser) or the riser down behind the tread (Extend Riser Behind Tread).
  • Nosing Length sets how far a tread runs past its riser; Extend Below Base moves the foot of the stringers (negative: below the base level); Tread Material, Riser Material, Stringer Material and Monolithic Material colour the parts; Break Symbol in Plan and Text Size control the plan symbol.
The type parameters of a stair

The landing stops behind the last riser of the run that reaches it, following its back face; in a monolithic stair it starts at the riser's face. In a monolithic stair whose top floor has its edge on the last riser, the run's underside goes on under that floor until it meets the floor's underside, as under a landing.

A section across the stair shows it cut with its slab. Volume in Properties and in the schedule of stairs is the volume of its solids.

The type's Text Font, Nosing Profile (Default or Rounded) and Apply Nosing Profile (front only, front and left, or front, left and right: past a side without a closed stringer), Open Stringer Offset, Trim Stringers at Top (Match Level stops the side stringers at the top level) and its identification (Code, Model, Manufacturer, Type Comments, URL, Description, Assembly Code) are in Type Parameters, as is a monolithic stair's Underside of Stringer (Smooth, a sloping slab, or Stepped: the slab follows the steps). Under Calculation Rules, Use Stair Calculator with a Target, Maximum and Minimum Result checks 2 risers + 1 tread: a stair outside the range is made, and a warning says so.

New in the realignment. In a stair's or a ramp's Properties, Show Up arrow in all views shows the whole arrow and UP in the top level's plan too. Desired number of risers can be typed: the risers become as high as the storey over that number (a number that would make them higher than the type's Maximum riser height is refused). When the risers drawn exceed the desired ones, or the Actual tread depth is under the type's minimum, the stair is made with a warning. With Use stair calculator on in the type, a new stair starts with the tread that gives the Target result. The Railing type dialog also offers Default, the Railing tool's type. In the sketch, each run's dashed run line has a grip at its end: dragged, it adds or removes risers. Work plane ▸ Set in a new stair's sketch puts it on another level. The UP/DN text is dragged by its grip also with the cursor over it, after Tab on the highlighted stair, and in the top level's plan. In the type: Stringer carriage height moves the side stringers under the treads, Landing stringer height is the height of the stringers that go on along the landings, Trim stringers at top also has Match landing stringer, and Landing overlap (stepped monolithic stairs) is how far the upright faces stand behind the risers; the type also has its Cost.

Stair calculator. In Type Properties, Calculation Rules is one row with its summary (for example «2 × A + 1 × P = 630 mm, 600–650») and the Edit… button, which opens Stair calculator: Use Stair Calculator, the riser's and the tread's multipliers (0.5 to 5, one decimal), Target Result, Maximum Result and Minimum Result. The selected stair's result updates at once, green within the range and red outside it; with a maximum under the minimum OK is off. OK gives the type the rules in one undo step; existing stairs keep their tread, new ones take it from the multipliers. In the BIMopen style the dialog has a preview.

docs.title: Ramps
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Vertical Links ▸ Ramp. Sketch mode starts with Run.
  2. Click where a run starts, then where it ends: it slopes at most the type's Ramp Max Slope (1/x) and rises at most its Maximum Incline Length (while drawing, a longer run stops there); the length made and left show beside the cursor.
  3. Draw the next run away from the end of the first: a landing joins them. Boundary and Riser draw a ramp by its lines, with a riser line at the start and the end of each run.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.

The type's Shape is Thick (its Thickness) or Solid (down to the base), and Ramp Material colours it. Its railings, Edit Sketch and Properties work as for stairs.

With Arc from Center and End in the Draw group, click the centre, the start of the run line and then its end round the centre: the run curves round it, two lines radiating from the centre at its ends and two boundary arcs at its sides. The type's Show Up Arrow in All Views draws the whole up arrow and UP in the plan of the top level too; its Text Font and identification are as for stairs.

docs.title: Railings
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Vertical Links ▸ Railing.
  2. Draw the path with Line: one chain of connected lines (a path in pieces, a closed path or one that goes back over itself is refused at Finish Edit Mode).
  3. To put the railing on a stair, click Tools ▸ Pick New Host and then the stair: the path drawn on it climbs with the stair.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.

Edit Path reopens a railing's path. Create ▸ Vertical Links ▸ Railing ▸ Place on a host puts a railing on each side of the stair or ramp you click: on the options bar Position chooses On treads (on the stair's edge) or On stringer (over the stringer, where the stair has one), Offset from Path moves it towards the inside of the stair and Invert switches between the two positions. The same two values are in the Properties of a stair's railing.

The railing's Type Parameters hold for every railing of that type: Railing Height (that of the top rail), Baluster Spacing, Baluster Offset (balusters and posts moved sideways) and the identity data; the preview shows the railing on a sample stair, seen from the side. Rail Structure (Non-Continuous) ▸ Edit… opens the list of the rails below the top one (Name, Height above the walking surface, Offset sideways, a square or round Profile) with Insert, Delete, Up and Down. Baluster Placement ▸ Edit… opens the Main pattern: the baluster or None, where it starts and ends (Host, Top rail or one of the rails) with their offsets, the distance between balusters, Break pattern at (at the end of each segment, at angles greater than a value, or never), Justify, Excess length fill and Use baluster per tread with how many on each tread; and the start, corner and end Posts (the post or None, its offsets, Space along the path, Offset sideways) with Corner posts at. The changes in these two windows apply with OK and are undone with a single Ctrl+Z. The Top rail, Handrail 1 and Handrail 2 rows are greyed: not available yet.

The type parameters of a railing, with the preview

The railings of a stair run on over its landings as one rail, at their height above the line of the nosings and above the landings. Where a run leaves a landing one riser higher, the type's Tangent Joins (the rail goes straight on) and Angled Joins (it turns) decide the join: Extend Rails to Meet (tangent joins only) carries the sloping rail on down to the landing, Add Vertical/Horizontal Segments rises upright at the first riser, No Connector leaves a gap.

The rails are mitred at every joint, where the path turns and where the slope changes: with Rail Connections Weld each rail is one piece, with Trim its pieces are cut on the joint's vertical plane. A post stands at the start and the end of each railing and at every change of direction in plan and wherever the slope changes, as where a run meets a landing. Use Landing Height Adjustment with Landing Height Adjustment raises (or lowers) the rail over the landings by that much.

A stair railing's path follows the stair's outline. Every post stands whole on the tread, landing or floor under it: where it would fall on a riser's line it moves by half its section, so no post sinks into the steps or hangs in front of the first one. Between two posts the balusters are evenly spaced, never wider apart than the spacing.

Place on a host works in plans and in the 3D view: the stair under the cursor shows where the two railings go. On stringer can be chosen only for a stair that has a stringer: on a monolithic stair it is greyed, on the options bar and in Properties. A new railing type has both Angled Joins and Tangent Joins set to Add Vertical/Horizontal Segments, Weld, no landing height adjustment, a bottom rail at 0.100 m (30×30), 20×20 balusters from the bottom rail to the top rail every 0.120 m, broken at the end of each segment and fitted to its length, and 50×50 posts standing on the host: where a run meets a landing the post stands on the landing at the riser's line, with the upright piece of the rail, and nothing runs over the treads. Where the rail rises upright at the start of a run, a low rail stays on the landing without entering the first tread.

New in the realignment. A railing's path is drawn with every tool of the Draw panel: an arc stays an arc in the railing, in 3D and in Edit Path, with posts only where it starts and ends. Pick New Host also takes a floor: the railing stands on its top. In Edit Path, with a line selected, the options bar offers Height correction (By type or Custom with its value) and Slope (By host, Flat, Sloped); Tools ▸ Edit Joins shows a box round the joint under the cursor, a click marks it with an X and Join in the options bar chooses how the rails meet there. In Rail structure each rail has its Material.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Component. The type selector lists the components loaded in the project; a preview follows the cursor, in plan and in the 3D view.
  2. Press Space to turn the preview by 90°.
  3. Click to place the component on the level of the plan.
A component follows the cursor before the click

Mode ▸ Load component opens the library, by folder (Furniture, Casework, Plumbing Fixtures): choose a component to see its types with their sizes (width × depth × height) and click Open to add them to the project.

Load component

Select a component and click Host ▸ Pick New Host, then a floor: the component moves onto the floor and stays on its top (click an empty point to put it back on the level). Its properties are Level, Host, Offset from Level, Rotation, Mark and Comments; Type Parameters has its width, depth, height and material.

docs.title: Casework
docs.text:
Casework is a category of its own, next to Furniture: the units fitted in kitchens and bathrooms. Its library folder has the Kitchen Unit (3.00 and 2.40 m long), the Wall Cabinet (60, 90 and 120 cm wide, 35 cm deep, 70 cm high), the Tall Cabinet 60 (60 × 60 cm, 2.10 m high), the Vanity Unit 80 and the Fitted Wardrobe; the free-standing Wardrobe stays furniture. A wall cabinet is placed 1.45 m above its level: its type's Default Offset says how high new ones go, and each keeps its own Offset from Level.

Casework is drawn by the view range of the plan, as walls are:

  • a unit the cut plane crosses (a tall cabinet, at the default 1.20 m) is cut: its outline with the cut line weight of the category, filled with its material's cut pattern;
  • a unit under the cut plane (the kitchen unit) is seen from above, in projection;
  • a unit over the cut plane and under the top of the view range (a wall cabinet) is seen from above too, dashed; over the top of the range it is not drawn.

Furniture and plumbing fixtures are never cut: they are drawn whole where the cut plane crosses them, and not drawn over it. So Visibility/Graphics and Object Styles give Casework its cut lines and cut patterns, and show «—» there for Furniture and Plumbing Fixtures. Casework has its own row in filters, schedules (Schedule/Quantities ▸ Casework), material takeoffs, project and shared parameters and legends. A project saved before casework had its own category opens with its kitchen units as casework, and the message of the opening says how many. Export IFC writes casework as furniture marked Casework; on import, furniture named as a cabinet, a counter, a vanity unit or a kitchen is proposed as casework.

docs.title: Schedules and IFC
docs.text: Floors, roofs, stairs, railings, furniture and casework have their schedules (Views ▸ Create ▸ Schedules ▸ Schedule/Quantities), one row per element. Export ▸ Export IFC4… writes floors as slabs (with their openings and slopes), roofs, stairs with their flights and landings, railings, furniture, casework and plumbing fixtures. A multistory stair is written once in each storey it is repeated in, with its railings.

docs.title: Not yet in BIMopen
docs.text: Slab edges, fascias and gutters come after this chapter's realignment. Ceilings have their own chapter, Ceilings and columns; shafts and openings cut in floors, roofs and walls are in Openings.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This chapter shows how to start BIMopen on the desktop and in the browser, what the sample project contains, and how to model a first small house: four walls, a door, a window, a floor, a roof, a 3D view and a sheet with the plan on it. It takes about ten minutes.

docs.title: Running BIMopen on the desktop
docs.text:
BIMopen is built from its source code with Rust, version 1.90 or later. On Linux the graphical interface also needs the development files of xkbcommon, Wayland and GTK 3.

sudo apt-get install -y libxkbcommon-dev libwayland-dev libgtk-3-dev   # Debian, Ubuntu
cargo run --release -p bimopen -- --sample                             # opens the sample house

The program is bimopen. It accepts a file to open and one option:

Command What it opens bimopen A new, empty project bimopen --sample The sample house bimopen house.bpr The project saved in house.bpr bimopen --no-splash As bimopen, without the start screen

You can also open a project by dragging a .bpr file from the file manager into the window.

docs.title: Start screen
docs.text:
While BIMopen loads, the start screen appears: a window without a frame, centred on the screen, with the name, the version, the loading stage under way with its percentage and a turquoise line growing along the bottom edge. The stages are the real ones (preferences, fonts, graphics card, families, opening the project); the screen stays at least half a second, so it does not flash, and fades out when the main window is ready. It speaks the language chosen in the app, otherwise the system's when it is one of the six, otherwise English.

To leave it out, clear Options ▸ General ▸ Show the start screen (BIMopen remembers it), or start bimopen --no-splash. On Wayland the compositor decides where the window appears (usually in the middle).

docs.title: Language and theme
docs.text:
The first time, BIMopen speaks the language of the operating system when it is one of its six languages (Italian, English, German, French, Spanish, Arabic), and English otherwise. To change it, click the gear at the right end of the top bar (Options) and choose the Language under User Interface. The interface changes at once.

In Options you also choose the Theme, Light or Dark (the sun or the moon in the top bar switches it too), and whether the background of the views is inverted (Invert background color: dark views with light lines). Choosing the dark theme also inverts the background; you can turn it back off. At the first start BIMopen uses the dark theme, with the background inverted. It remembers the language, the theme and the background for the next time.

docs.title: Running BIMopen in the browser
docs.text:
The web version is the same program, compiled for the browser. Open bimopen.it/app/: it starts with the sample house. Nothing needs to be installed, and the project stays in your browser: it is not sent anywhere.

The address accepts these options, which can be combined with &:

Address Effect app/?lang=de Opens in German for this visit (it, en, de, fr, es, ar) app/?empty Starts with a new, empty project instead of the sample app/?webgl Draws with WebGL2 even where WebGPU is available

The browser must support WebGPU or WebGL2. In the browser some things work differently:

  • Open… cannot show a file dialog: drag a .bpr file into the page to open it;
  • Save and the exports download the file, with the name of the project.

To build the web version yourself:

cargo xtask web                              # builds dist/web
python3 -m http.server 8080 -d dist/web      # then open http://localhost:8080

cargo xtask web needs the wasm32-unknown-unknown target of Rust and the wasm-bindgen command of the version written in Cargo.lock; with binaryen's wasm-opt installed, the result is smaller.

docs.title: The sample project
docs.text:
The sample house shows most of what BIMopen can do. Open it with File ▸ Sample project (the File panel opens from BIMopen's mark, at the top of the rail), with bimopen --sample, or by typing sample at the command line.

It contains:

  • two levels, each with its floor plan, and five grid lines;
  • fourteen walls of four types, with layers, joined at the corners;
  • six doors and twelve windows, tagged in the plans;
  • two floors, a pitched roof, a stair with its railings and a storefront curtain wall;
  • furniture and plumbing fixtures, eight rooms coloured by use, with a legend;
  • a section, an elevation, an area plan, a saved 3D view and a free 2D view with a wall detail;
  • dimensions, text notes and the schedules of walls, doors, windows, rooms and materials;
  • its place in Cagliari, where its address is: the sun and the shadows are those of that city.

Tip

The sample is a good place to try a tool before using it on your own project: a new sample is always one click away, and nothing you change in it is saved unless you save it.

docs.title: Your first house
docs.text: The steps below start from an empty project and end with a sheet. Every step names what to click in the BIMopen interface style, the one BIMopen starts in; the interface chapter explains each part of the window.

docs.title: 1. Start a new project
docs.text:
1. Click BIMopen's mark at the top of the rail: the File panel opens.
  2. Click New… in the Projects group. The New project dialog proposes BIMopen's default template: click OK.
Step 1: the File panel

The new project has two levels, Ground Floor and First Floor, a floor plan for each, and the default 3D view. It has no walls yet. Its wall, door, window, floor and roof types are ready to use.

docs.title: 2. Open the ground floor plan
docs.text:
In the views strip under the drawing area, click the thumbnail Floor Plan: Ground Floor. The plan opens in the drawing area, and the top bar and the view selector show Floor Plan: Ground Floor.

Note

Views on the rail also shows the Project Index, the tree of every view: there, a single click on a view shows its properties in the element panel without opening it, and a double-click opens it.

docs.title: 3. Draw four walls
docs.text:
1. In the tools of Create, the rail entry BIMopen opens with, click Wall in the Build group (if the tool panel is folded, click Create on the rail first). The contextual card Draw Wall comes on top of the tool panel, the options strip over the view shows the settings of the wall, and the element panel shows the type of the next wall, Exterior wall - Clay block 300 + ETICS.
  2. In the status bar, turn on Ortho: the walls stay horizontal or vertical.
  3. Click in the plan where the first corner goes. The status bar asks for the next point: WALL next point [Esc to finish]:.
  1. Click the second, third and fourth corners. While you move the mouse, the length and the angle of the wall being drawn are shown next to it.
  2. Click the first corner again: the four walls are joined at the corners.
  3. Press Esc to stop the chain, and Esc again to end the tool.

Tip

You can draw the same walls by typing their corners in metres: wall 0,0 10,0 10,6 0,6 c. The final c closes the chain. See Command line and MCP.

docs.title: 4. Add a door and a window
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Door, then click on a wall where the door goes. The door is placed in the wall, which is cut around it. The command log confirms it: Door «Single swing door 80x210» in wall ….
  2. Press Esc: the tool ends and the contextual card goes away.
  3. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Window, click on another wall, and press Esc.

A door or a window can only be placed in a wall: after a click away from the walls, the command line answers no wall at that point and nothing is placed.

docs.title: 5. Add a floor and a roof
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Flooring. Sketch mode opens: the contextual card Edit | Create Floor Boundary, with Pick Walls active.
  2. Move the cursor over a wall and press Tab: the four walls are highlighted. Click: their lines go on the inner faces of the walls.
  3. Click Finish Edit Mode: the floor is made and the command log gives its area.
  4. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Roof. Pick Walls is active again; the options strip has Defines Slope (ticked) and the Overhang (500 mm by default).
  5. Press Tab over a wall, click, then Finish Edit Mode: a hip roof sloping at 30° covers the walls, with the overhang all around.
Step 5: walls, door, window, floor and roof

Floors, roofs, stairs and components tells more about sketch mode.

docs.title: 6. Look at it in 3D
docs.text:
Click the {3D} thumbnail in the views strip. The default 3D view, {3D}, opens. Drag with the right mouse button (or with Shift and the middle button) to orbit, drag with the middle button to pan, and turn the wheel to zoom; the left button selects, as in plans. Home fits the whole model in the view.

Step 6: the house in 3D

docs.title: 7. Put the plan on a sheet
docs.text:
1. Click Document on the rail, then Sheet in the Sheets group. The New Sheet dialog lists the title blocks: none, A0, A1, A2 or A3, with their size in millimetres.
  2. Click OK. The sheet is created with the next free number (A101 for the first one, then A102…) and opens.
  3. Click Document ▸ Sheets ▸ View. The Views dialog lists the views that are not on a sheet yet.
  4. Choose Floor Plan: Ground Floor and click Add View to Sheet. A rectangle of the plan's size follows the cursor: click on the sheet where the plan goes. It is placed at its own scale, 1 : 100, as a viewport, which stays selected.
Step 7: the plan on a sheet

docs.title: 8. Undo, redo and save
docs.text:
• Ctrl+Z undoes the last change (here, the viewport goes away); Ctrl+Y redoes it. The arrows of the top bar, Undo and Redo, do the same.
  • Ctrl+S saves the project, as a click on the save state in the top bar. A project that has never been saved asks for a file name first; the file has the extension .bpr. In the browser, the file is downloaded.

The top bar says Unsaved changes while there are changes to save, and Saved after saving.

docs.title: What next
docs.text:
• The interface describes every part of the window.
  • Keyboard shortcuts lists the keys and the two-letter shortcuts, such as WA for a wall.
  • Command line and MCP shows how to type commands, run scripts and let an agent model for you.

docs.title: Importing and converting
docs.text: A model made with other software arrives as an IFC file. BIMopen reads its walls, floors, doors, windows and spaces as its own elements. Everything else with a shape (roofs, beams, columns, stairs, railings, curtain walls, furniture, fittings) is kept as an imported object: its geometry as it was read, as a generic model. Convert then makes each imported object a BIMopen element of any category, when and as far as you need it.

docs.title: Opening an IFC file
docs.text:
1. Open the File panel (BIMopen's mark at the top of the rail) and choose Open… ➤ IFC….
  2. Pick an IFC2x3 or IFC4 file.

BIMopen makes a new project: storeys become levels, walls are rebuilt from their axis, slabs become floors, doors and windows go in the walls their openings cut, spaces become rooms. Every other object with a shape becomes an imported object. Each one remembers:

  • the file it came from and its format (casa.ifc · IFC4);
  • its IFC class (IfcRoof, IfcFurniture…) and its identifier;
  • the object it is a part of: the flights of a stair, the panels of a curtain wall;
  • its property sets and quantities, shown in Properties under IFC Properties.

The messages count what was read, what was approximated and what was left out.

docs.title: Import IFC Options
docs.text:
Coordinate ▸ IFC Options… opens Import IFC Options: what each IFC class becomes when a file is opened.

Each IFC class, its category and what happens on opening
  • Walls, slabs, doors, windows and spaces are read as BIMopen elements; any of them can be read as an imported object instead (Generic Models) or left out (Not Imported).
  • The other classes are read as imported objects. Category is the category each class is proposed as when it is converted, any category BIMopen has.
  • On Opening says what happens to them as the file opens: To Convert leaves them for later; Keep the geometry, Rebuild as a BIMopen element or Create a component converts them at once (see below).
  • Add Class adds a class the list does not have.
  • Load… reads a class mapping file, Save As… writes one: a text file, one class a line. Default puts the standard mapping back.

The options are kept between sessions.

docs.title: Importing an IFC file into the project
docs.text:
Open ➤ IFC… makes a new project. Link and import ▸ Import IFC brings the file into the open project instead, which already has its levels and types: converting is faster, because Convert… proposes the project's types first.

  1. Link and import ▸ Import IFC (or File ▸ Open ▸ Import IFC…, or Ctrl+K, «import ifc»), then pick the file.
  2. In the Import IFC dialog:
  3. Placement: Auto - Origin to Origin (the usual case), Center to Center, or Manual: after Import you click the point in a plan where the file's origin goes.
  4. Levels: each storey of the file goes to a project level, by name and then by elevation (±100 mm), or to a new level; the choice can be changed row by row.
  5. Classes to import: the file's classes with their objects and the category proposed; untick those not needed. Spaces become rooms only if you choose so.
  6. Project types: Propose the project's types first (on) and Convert at once when the match is high.
  7. Already imported from this file: on a second import of the same file, Update compares the identifiers (GUIDs): it adds the new ones, updates the changed ones, and reports those no longer there without removing them; or Import as a copy.
  8. Import. It is all one Undo step; Conversion Status turns on in the view.
Import IFC: the file's storeys go to the project's levels

Walls, floors, doors and windows come in as imported objects too, to be converted into the project's types. In Convert…, Type lists the project's types ranked by match, the first marked ★: the category, the thickness or sizes (the same within 5 mm) and the name (the same, or words in common). Each row says how well it matches (high from 85, medium from 60, low) and why; the first is already chosen if the match is at least medium, otherwise New type from object. Converting a whole class, one row for each type of the file says which project type it becomes.

The project's types, the closest first

docs.title: Conversion Status
docs.text:
While the project holds imported objects still to convert, the view bar shows Conversion Status, with their number. Its tooltip says how many there are and in how many IFC classes.

Conversion Status in the view bar

Click it: the view shows each object in the colour of where it stands, inside a teal frame.

Colour Status Meaning Orange To Convert imported, still a generic model Yellow Category Assigned the imported geometry kept, with a category Green Converted a BIMopen element or a component instance Red Not Recognised a rebuild did not recognise the shape: geometry only Grey Born in BIMopen not imported Conversion Status in the 3D view, with its panel

It works in plans, sections, elevations and 3D views, and only changes the window: the model and the other views stay as they are. While it is on, only imported objects can be selected.

The same in a plan

The panel Conversion Status, under Properties, has:

  • the legend with the count of each status: a click on a status hides it in the view, or shows it again;
  • the IFC classes with objects still to convert, the category each is proposed as and how many are left. A click on a class selects its objects to convert and opens Convert….

When nothing is left to convert, the panel says so. Turn Conversion Status off and its button leaves the view bar.

In the Classic style the panel is a tab beside Properties; in touch mode it is a sheet, opened from the view's settings.

docs.title: Converting an imported object
docs.text:
Select one or more imported objects: the contextual card Edit | Imported Objects opens. Convert… opens Convert Imported Object.

The roof, rebuilt as a BIMopen roof
  1. Category: what the object becomes. The class's proposal comes first.
  2. One of the three ways (below). A way that does not apply to the category is greyed.
  3. Type: one of the category's types (the project's first, ranked by match), or a new type made from the object.
  4. Detected: what BIMopen reads in the shape and how sure it is.
  5. Parameters: Mark and Comments, and the object's IFC properties.
  6. Convert.

The preview shows what the object will be. The Preview switch in the header hides it; the dialog keeps its size.

docs.title: The three ways
docs.text:
Way Categories What happens Keep the geometry all The object takes the category, a type and parameters. It counts in schedules, filters, visibility and the IFC export as an element of that category; its shape stays the imported one. It can be moved, rotated and mirrored. Rebuild as a BIMopen element walls, floors, roofs, doors, windows BIMopen reads the shape and makes the native element, edited like one drawn: a wall's axis, thickness and height; a floor's outline, thickness and top; a roof's outline, slopes, thickness and eave height; a door or window in the wall it stands in, with its width, height and sill. Create a component furniture, plumbing fixtures, generic models, doors, windows, columns, beams The geometry becomes a component type with Width, Depth and Height from its overall size; changing them stretches the shape. The object becomes its instance.

A shape that cannot be rebuilt as the chosen category turns red (Not Recognised) and stays as it was: convert it again keeping its geometry. Rebuilding columns, beams, stairs and railings comes in a later phase.

When it rebuilds, BIMopen carries the file's materials into the native element: the layers of a wall, floor or roof with their thickness, the frame and glass of a window. A material the project already has with the same name is used as it is; a new one takes the file's colour and the hatch patterns of a similar material. A wall that turns a corner becomes one wall per stretch; a roof with planes at different heights, one roof per plane. The covering, ridges and gutters on a roof go with the new roof, and the walls the roof cuts are attached to it. Restore Original puts everything back as it was.

Category in Properties does the same as Keep the geometry: choosing a category there converts the selected object at once.

Converted objects turn green

docs.title: Components from imported objects
docs.text:
Create Component on the contextual card opens the dialog with Create a component chosen.

A chair becomes a component; its three copies become instances

The IFC properties that every copy has alike become type parameters; those that differ stay with each instance. The component appears in the Project Index under Imported Objects, and its Type Parameters change every instance at once.

docs.title: Identical shapes
docs.text: Copies of one shape, moved and rotated in plan, are recognised as identical. Select Identical Shapes selects them; in the dialog, Also apply to the N identical shapes in the project converts them together (on by default when making a component). As instances of one component they take less memory and draw faster on large models.

docs.title: Selecting imported objects
docs.text:
• Select Class selects the imported objects of the same IFC class.
  • A class in the panel Conversion Status, or Convert All (N)… on a class in the Project Index, selects its objects to convert and opens the dialog.
  • An object that is a part of another one (a flight of a stair) goes with it: converting the whole takes its parts.

docs.title: Imported objects in the Project Index
docs.text:
Imported Objects in the Project Index lists each file read, with its format and how many objects are left to convert; under it the IFC classes, under each class its objects, with the colour of their status and, once converted, the category they became. Objects made of parts list their parts under them.

Imported Objects in the Project Index
  • Only to convert hides what is already converted.
  • A click on an object selects it; a double click shows it in a view.
  • The right button on a class: Convert All (N)…, Select All to Convert (N), Restore Originals (N).
  • The right button on a file: the same, and Remove Source References….
  • The right button on an object: Convert…, Select Identical Shapes, Show in View, Conceal in view, Restore Original.

docs.title: Restoring the originals
docs.text:
What a conversion replaces is kept in the project, in the .bpr file: the original object, with the parts it took along. Restore Original (on the contextual card, in the Project Index or in the right button's menu) puts it back as it was imported, orange again.

Restoring asks first

It asks first, and says what will be lost: changes made to rebuilt elements or components, and doors and windows hosted in converted walls. A component made by the conversion goes with its last instance. Undo takes back a conversion or a restore like any other change.

The originals' geometry is stored once for every identical mesh, so keeping them costs little. When the conversions are final, Remove Source References… on the file in the Project Index deletes the originals: after it, Restore Original is no longer possible.

docs.title: Coming next
docs.text:
• Link IFC: the file as a read-only reference, reloaded when it changes; placement by shared coordinates.
  • Update from File: reading the source file again and updating its objects.
  • Tools by face, to place walls, floors and roofs on free and curved forms.
  • Rebuilding columns, beams, stairs and railings.
  • Converting objects from OBJ and glTF files with the same dialog.

docs.title: Interface styles
docs.text:
BIMopen has two interface styles and a touch mode. All of them run the same commands, with the same names, keyboard shortcuts and results; only the look and the place of the tools change.

  • The BIMopen style, described in The interface and pictured throughout this manual: the rail, the tool panel, the command search, the element panel and the strip of views. BIMopen starts in this style.
  • The Classic style: the ribbon with its tabs, the options bar, the Properties palette and the Project Index in panels.
  • Touch mode: the layout for touch screens and pens, on a touch monitor, a tablet or a phone.

docs.title: Choosing the style
docs.text:
1. Click the gear at the right end of the top bar, or open the File panel and choose Options.
  2. Under User Interface, set Interface to Classic or BIMopen. BIMopen starts in the BIMopen style.

The window changes at once. The choice is remembered, on the desktop and in the browser, and the next session starts in the same style. Theme (Light or Dark) applies to both styles.

The BIMopen style in the dark theme

In Arabic the whole window is mirrored, in every style: the rail and the tool panel, or the palettes, are on the right, the element panel on the left.

docs.title: The Classic style
docs.text:
The Classic style Part Where What it holds Title bar Top The quick access toolbar (Open…, Save, Undo, Redo and the tools you add), the project and the active view, the light or dark theme and the ? menu Ribbon Under the title bar File, which opens the File panel, then the tabs (Model, Structure, Reinforced concrete, Metal, Prefabrication, MEP, Link and import, Annotations, Check, Massing & site, Collaborate, Views, Project) with their groups of buttons, and the contextual tab while a tool works or something is selected Options bar Under the ribbon The options of the active tool, as the options strip of the BIMopen style, and at its right end what the tool expects or the element under the cursor, the selection count and Select and Drag; right-click it for Dock at Bottom Properties and Project Index Left The element panel's Properties tab, and the Project Index of Views, as panels that dock on either side or float Drawing area Centre The views, each with its view control bar at the bottom (scale, detail, crop, isolate) and the navigation bar on its right edge (Zoom to Fit, Zoom In, Zoom Out, Zoom Options) Command line Under the drawing area The log and the prompt; what you type in a view goes there Views and components strip Bottom The same strip as in the BIMopen style

The rail of the BIMopen style lists the same tabs as the ribbon, with the same names and in the same order, and the contextual tab as Edit; Views also holds the Project Index.

docs.title: Everything of the Classic style
docs.text:
Every function of the Classic style is in the BIMopen style, once:

  • every button of the ribbon is a tile of the tool panel, under the same tab of the rail and in the same group, and the contextual tab is Edit on the rail, chosen by itself while a tool works or something is selected;
  • BIMopen's mark at the top of the rail opens the File panel; the top bar has undo, redo, the quick access tools and the ? menu;
  • Views holds the whole Project Index, with its menus;
  • a thumbnail of the view strip can be dragged onto the open sheet, or onto a sheet's thumbnail, and its right-click menu has the browser's actions and Open in the active window;
  • the view selector's menu arranges the view windows (Switch View, Tile, Cascade, Maximize, Replicate, Close Hidden); Ctrl+Tab goes to the previous window;
  • the right button on a tile offers Add to Quick Access Toolbar: the tool shows in the top bar, works whatever tab is open, and its right button offers Remove from Quick Access Toolbar;
  • the key tips work as on the ribbon: tap Alt (or press F10), then a tab's letter opens that tab on the rail (its letter shows on the rail) and a tool's letters start it.

docs.title: Touch mode
docs.text: Touch mode lays the interface out for touch screens and pens: phones, tablets and touch monitors. It runs the same commands as the two styles, with the same names; only the layout changes, and every control is big enough for a finger.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Options ▸ User Interface ▸ Touch mode has three values:

Value Effect Automatic On where the device is touch first: in a browser with a finger as pointer or a window at most 900 pixels wide, and on Android. On the desktop it stays off Always Always on, on the desktop too (a touch monitor, a tablet PC) Never Never on

BIMopen remembers the choice with the other preferences. Menu ▸ Leave touch mode brings back the other interface until the next start.

docs.title: Phone, landscape and tablet
docs.text:
The layout follows the room the window has.

On a touch monitor, or any wide window (here 1920 × 1080): the rail on the left opens a palette of tools for each category (Model, Structure, MEP, Annotations, Views, Project), the properties stay on the right, the views and components strip at the bottom, and the Command or search field in the top bar, beside Undo, Redo and Pen.

Touch mode on a touch monitor, 1920 × 1080

On a tablet, upright (800 × 1280) or sideways (1280 × 800): the same layout as on a monitor. Where the window is narrow the properties are put away, to leave the room to the drawing: Properties in the top bar brings them back.

Touch mode on a tablet held upright, 800 × 1280 Touch mode on a tablet held sideways, 1280 × 800

On a phone, upright (narrow and tall): a compact top bar with the menu, the project and the view (a tap opens the views), Undo, Redo, Command or search and Pen; the drawing takes the whole width; five big buttons at the bottom, Views, Components, Tools (Modify while something is selected), Properties and Commands, each opening a sheet from the bottom. Drag the sheet's handle up to make it taller, down to make it smaller or close it; a tap outside closes it.

Touch mode on a phone held upright, 412 × 915
