• Hardware acceleration: Automatic uses the graphics card where there is one and, if it is missing or does not start, draws on the processor; Always on never falls back to the processor (without a graphics card the 3D views say so instead of drawing: useful to find a faulty driver); Off (processor only) draws the 3D views on the processor, for faulty drivers (black screen, flickering), more slowly on large models.
  • Graphics card: Automatic (the dedicated one, if there is one), the dedicated or the integrated card, by name; on laptops the integrated one uses less power. The card is chosen when BIMopen starts: after a change the tab says to restart BIMopen. A card that cannot draw in the window is greyed, with the reason; if the chosen card is missing or cannot draw, BIMopen uses the automatic one, says so and goes back to Automatic. In a browser and on Android the browser or the system chooses it.
  • In use shows the card and the graphics API really in use (for example Vulkan, Direct3D 12, Metal, WebGPU, WebGL2), or the processor and why.
  • 3D view ▸ Edges: Automatic edges follow the view instantly, also right after a change; Exact edges are the same as in print, slower on large models. Printing and export always use the exact ones, as do the Wireframe style, Sketchy Lines and views without acceleration or on WebGL2. Each 3D view also has its own Edges property: As in Options, Automatic or Exact.

At the command line: graphicsettings {"acceleration":"automatica|sempre|disattivata","adapter":"automatica|dedicata|integrata","edges":"automatici|esatti","antialias":true} (without arguments it reports the settings in use); a 3D view's edges with graphicoptions {"edges3d":"opzioni|automatici|esatti"}.

docs.title: Copying settings from a project
docs.text:
Settings ➤ Settings ➤ Copy Settings from Project copies settings from another project into this one. In Select Items To Copy, choose the project with Browse… (Copy from:), then tick what to copy: the types of walls, floors, roofs, doors and windows, stairs, railings, curtain panels and mullions, line styles, filled region types, materials, fill and line patterns, line weights, styles by category, view templates, filters, viewport types, title blocks, the project units, the print settings and the project information (Check all, None).

Copying settings from another project

What is copied brings along what it uses: a wall type its materials, a material its patterns, a view template its filters. When names are already in the project, Duplicate Types asks whether to Overwrite them or to transfer the New Only. The whole transfer is one step of undo.

docs.title: Exporting to IFC
docs.text:
File ➤ Export ➤ IFC… writes the model in IFC4: walls with their axis and body, openings, doors, windows, floors, roofs, stairs, railings, curtain walls, furniture and rooms as spaces, on their storeys.

Export ➤ Options ➤ IFC Options… opens IFC Export Classes: the IFC class of each category; Not Exported leaves a category out, and Default goes back to the standard classes. The classes are kept with the project.

docs.title: Opening IFC files
docs.text:
File ➤ Open… ➤ IFC… makes a new project from an IFC2x3 or IFC4 file, in metres or millimetres: storeys become levels, walls are rebuilt from their axis (or from the long side of their body), slabs become floors, doors and windows go in the walls their openings cut, and spaces become rooms. The messages count what was not read.

Open ➤ IFC Options… opens Import IFC Options: what each IFC class becomes (walls, floors, doors, windows, rooms or Not Imported), and Default. The choices are kept between sessions.

Objects with a shape that are not walls, floors, doors, windows or spaces are kept as imported objects, to convert: see Importing and converting.

docs.title: Exporting to USD
docs.text:
File ➤ Export ➤ USD… saves the active 3D view as a USD scene, an open format read by rendering, animation and augmented reality programs. When the active view is not 3D, {3D} is exported. Elements and categories hidden in the view are left out, and with the section box on, so are the elements wholly outside the box. The scene is arranged by level, category and element, in metres with the Z axis up.

  • .usdz is a single file holding the scene and the materials' textures; .usda is the scene as text, without textures.
  • Materials: colour, roughness, metallic, transparency and the appearance's images, as in the Realistic view.
  • BIM properties: category, type, level, mark, IFC identifier and parameters of every element.
  • Identical shapes as instances: identical doors, windows and components are written once.
  • The view's camera and The view's sun and sky.
  • Naming: Manual uses the name typed in Name/prefix (or the project's), Automatic - long adds the view's type and name to the prefix, Automatic - short uses only the view's type and name.

The choices stay for the next time.

docs.title: Project bundles
docs.text:
File ➤ Export ➤ Share ➤ Project bundle… gathers the project and the files it uses into a single .zip file: linked models (with the files they use), the source files of imported objects, type catalogues. The dialog lists every file with its state: not found when it is missing beside the project, to add on the web, where the browser cannot see the folder. Add files… puts other documents in the bundle, such as a report or a specification. The bundle takes the project as it is now, unsaved changes included. Components and material images are already inside the project.

Inside the .zip all files sit at the same level and the project refers to them by name, so the bundle works wherever it is unpacked. The Bundle report.txt says what was included and what was missing. Purge unused types, Remove worksets and Remove sheets change only the copy in the bundle. With Save settings for next use the choices stay for the next time.

File ➤ Open… ➤ Project bundle…, or Project… choosing the .zip, unpacks the bundle into a folder beside it with the same name and opens the project. On the web the project opens from memory.

docs.title: Other exports
docs.text: Printing to PDF and exporting images are described in Sheets, schedules and printing; schedules export as delimited text from the same chapter. bimopen-cli convert exports from the command line (see Command line and MCP).

docs.title: Selecting and modifying
docs.text: Before most changes you select what to change. This chapter describes how elements are highlighted and selected, how a selection is refined, how selected elements are dragged, and the tools of the Modify group. Everything here works the same in the desktop app and in the browser.

docs.title: Highlighting and selecting
docs.text:
A wall selected in the plan: its contextual card on the left, its properties in the element panel on the right

Move the cursor over an element: its lines are drawn wider, the status bar at the bottom of the window names it (category and type, as Walls : Exterior wall…), and after a moment the same words appear under the cursor. Click to select the highlighted element. A selected element is drawn in the selection colour in every view where it shows, and the count at the right end of the status bar says how many elements are selected.

A right click on an element selects it and opens the context menu. Esc, or a click on an empty spot, clears the selection.

To… Do this add an element to the selection Ctrl + click take an element out of the selection Shift + click select what is wholly inside a window drag from left to right select what a window touches drag from right to left (the window is dashed) add, or take away, what a window catches drag with Ctrl, or with Shift select again what was selected before Ctrl+Left, or right click ▸ Select Previous A window from right to left selects what it touches

Windows work in plans, sections, sheets and 3D views. In a 3D view the left button selects; the right button orbits and the middle button pans (see The interface).

docs.title: Elements close together: TAB
docs.text: When elements lie close together or one over the other, the one highlighted may not be the one you want. Keep the cursor still and press Tab: the next element under the cursor is highlighted and the status bar names it. Shift+Tab goes back. Click to select the highlighted element. In a 3D view Tab goes from the nearest element to the ones behind it; on a sheet, through views placed one over the other.

docs.title: Chains of walls and lines
docs.text:
Walls and lines joined end to end form a chain. With the cursor on one of them, Tab highlights the whole chain (the status bar says Chain of n joined elements); a click selects it. A chain can mix walls with room separators and area outlines; detail lines chain with the detail lines of their view. Where three or more meet, the chain goes on along the one that makes the smallest angle with the last; a wall that stops against another one between its ends takes the chain on along that wall.

TAB: the whole chain of walls

Part of a chain. Select the first element of the part, move the cursor over the last one and press Tab: the elements between them are highlighted. Tab again highlights the whole chain, a third time the last element alone. Click to select what is highlighted. On a closed chain the part goes round by the side where the cursor is: near the end of the last element that one way round reaches first.

Elements joined at a point. Select an element and keep the cursor on it, near an end where others are joined. Tab highlights it with the nearest one joined there; Tab again, every element joined there. Click to select them.

A selected chain. Where two selected walls or lines meet, a round control appears. Drag it to move the joint: the selected ends there move together and stay joined; elements not selected are left where they are. Drag the chain with Shift to move it whole, horizontally or vertically; drag it with Ctrl to place a copy.

docs.title: Filtering a selection
docs.text:
Click the count in the status bar, or Filter on the contextual card, to open Filter. It lists the categories in the selection, how many elements each has, and the total. Untick a category to leave its elements out: the selection and the count in the status bar follow at once. Check all and Check none tick or untick every category. OK keeps the selection, Cancel brings back the one you started with.

Filter

docs.title: Select All Instances
docs.text: Right-click an element ▸ Select All Instances, then Visible in View (the elements of the same type shown in the active view) or In Entire Project. Typing SA and Enter does the same as Visible in View. The element must have a type: rooms, for example, have none.

docs.title: Dragging elements
docs.text:
Drag a selected element to move it; the whole selection moves together, and one drag is undone by one Ctrl+Z. A temporary dimension shows the move, and the status bar its length (Move: 1500). With Select and Drag turned on in the status bar, an element can be dragged without selecting it first; with it off, a drag that starts on an element not selected draws a window.

  • A wall joined at its ends to walls that are not selected moves square to itself only, and the joined walls stretch to stay joined. Walls that stop against it follow too. Hold Shift to move it freely; the joined walls still follow.
  • Any other element moves freely; hold Shift to keep the move horizontal or vertical.
  • Doors and windows move with their wall and keep their place along it. Dragged on their own, they slide along the wall; dropped on another wall, they move into it.
  • Hold Ctrl when you start dragging to place a copy instead.

Elements are dragged in plans, sections and elevations (along the view), on sheets (views), and in 3D views, where they move on the horizontal plane where you grabbed them. The arrow keys move the selection a small step, rounded to a tidy value at the zoom of the view; with Shift, ten steps.

docs.title: The Modify tools
docs.text:
The Modify group of the contextual card has three rows: Align, Offset, Mirror on Axis, Mirror on Line, Split Element, Split with Joint; Move, Copy, Rotate, Shorten/Lengthen, Shorten/Lengthen one element, Shorten/Lengthen several elements; Repeat in Series, Scale, Fix, Unpin, Delete. The status bar says what each tool expects next, and the options strip shows its options. Esc cancels the step in progress; pressed again, it ends the tool.

Move, Copy, Rotate, the two Mirror tools, Repeat in Series and Scale work on the selection. Started with nothing selected, they let you select first (clicks, Ctrl, windows, Tab), then go on when you press Enter or End on the options strip.

Move, Copy and Rotate also work in 3D views: their points are taken on the plane of the level clicked.

Before each click the tool shows what the click would do: the selection drawn where it would go (moved, copied, turned, mirrored about the axis under the cursor, offset to the cursor's side, aligned to the reference), following the cursor, with the distance or the angle beside it.

Where a tool asks for a second point, you can type a distance (or an angle) instead and press Enter: it shows next to the cursor while you type, and is measured towards the cursor.

docs.title: Move
docs.text:
Click a base point, then the destination. The tool ends and the elements stay selected. Options:

Move: the preview, then the result
  • Constrain: the move is along or square to the selected wall (horizontal or vertical for other elements);
  • Disjoin: walls joined to the moved ones do not follow, and a door or window can be moved onto another wall;
  • Copy: copies are placed instead; with Multiple, one at each click until Esc.

docs.title: Copy
docs.text: As Move, but a copy is placed. With Multiple, a copy at each click until Esc; Constrain as for Move.

docs.title: Rotate
docs.text:
The centre of rotation shows at the middle of the selection; drag it to put it elsewhere. Click the first ray, then the second: the selection turns by the angle between them, shown by a temporary angular dimension. Instead of the second ray, type the angle and press Enter, or type it in Angle on the options strip and press Enter. Copy turns a copy; without Disjoin, walls joined to the turned ones follow.

Rotate: the angle before the second click

docs.title: Mirror
docs.text: Mirror on Axis: click a wall, a grid or a line as the axis. Mirror on Line: click two points. Copy is ticked: a mirrored copy is placed; untick it to mirror the elements themselves.

docs.title: Repeat in Series
docs.text:
Linear: click two points. Number is how many elements in all. With Move To: 2° the two points give the spacing; with Last, the last element goes to the second point and the others are spread evenly. Constrain keeps the direction along or square to the selection.

Radial: drag the centre where the copies turn about, click the first ray, then the second (or type the angle and press Enter, also in Angle). With 2° the angle is between neighbours, with Last it is the whole span.

docs.title: Offset
docs.text:
Moves a wall or a line square to itself, or places a copy (Copy is ticked).

  • Numerical: set Offset, then click the element on the side it should go to. Press Tab first to offset the whole chain (of the same category) as one: its corners are kept.
  • Graphical: click the element (Tab for the chain), then two points: the distance between them, square to the element, is the offset. You can type it instead. Ctrl copies.

docs.title: Align
docs.text:
Click the reference, then the element to align: the face of the element nearest to your click goes onto the face of the reference nearest to its click. Prefer chooses Wall faces or Wall centerlines. After aligning, a padlock shows on the aligned face: click it to keep the two aligned, so that moving the reference moves the other one too. Without Multiple Alignment the next click picks a new reference; with it (or holding Ctrl) you can align several elements to the same one. Esc once starts a new alignment, twice ends the tool.

A wall aligned and locked to a grid follows it when you move the grid, in 3D too, and the walls joined to its ends stretch or shorten and stay joined. With Moves with nearby elements, in a component's properties, the component moves with the nearest wall, at the same distance.

docs.title: Shorten/Lengthen
docs.text:
Walls and lines are trimmed or extended; click each one on the part to keep.

  • Shorten/Lengthen: two elements, which then meet at a corner;
  • Shorten/Lengthen one element: the boundary, then the element;
  • Shorten/Lengthen several elements: the boundary, then each element in turn.

docs.title: Split Element and Split with Joint
docs.text: Split Element: click a wall or a line where it should become two. With Delete Inner Segment, click two points: the part between them is removed, with the doors and windows in it. Split with Joint: set Joint Gap, then click: the two parts are that far apart.

docs.title: Scale
docs.text: Walls and lines (and the position of dimensions) can be scaled; with anything else selected, Scale is not available. Graphical: click the origin, the end of a first vector, the end of a second one: the elements are scaled by the ratio of the two lengths (you can type the second one). Numerical: set Scale Factor, then click the origin. Doors and windows keep their distance from the middle of their wall.

docs.title: Fix and Unpin
docs.text: Fix keeps the selected elements where they are: they cannot be dragged, moved by a tool or deleted, and a message says so. A pinned element shows a pushpin when selected; click the pushpin, or use Unpin, to free it.

docs.title: Delete, undo and redo
docs.text: Delete (or the Del key) removes the selection and what it hosts; pinned elements stay. Ctrl+Z undoes the last change and Ctrl+Y redoes it: each tool, drag or nudge is one step.

docs.title: Copy, cut and paste
docs.text:
Copy to clipboard (Ctrl+C) puts the selection on the clipboard; Cut to clipboard (Ctrl+X) puts it there and takes it out of the project. Paste (Ctrl+V) brings it back. The three buttons are in the Modify group of the contextual card, next to the other ways of Paste; in the Classic style, in the Clipboard panel. The keys act while no tool is active and no field is being edited.

In a plan, Paste shows the lines of what was copied at the cursor: they follow it, and a click drops them there. The elements pasted stay selected. Pressed outside a plan, Ctrl+V pastes in the same place.

The other ways of Paste (in the Classic style, in its drop-down) keep the elements where they were and need no point:

Way Where the elements go Paste on the chosen levels The model elements, in the same place, on each level ticked Paste in the chosen views The elements of a view (lines, texts, dimensions…), in each view ticked, of the same kind as the one they come from Paste in the active view In the same place, in the open view and at its level Paste in the same place Where they were, also in another project Paste on the clicked level In a section or an elevation: the level nearest the click is highlighted with its name; the click pastes on it

The two ways with "chosen" open a window with a Search field over the list of levels or views; tick the ones you want and click OK. A way that cannot paste what the clipboard holds in the open view is greyed, and the status bar says why.

  • Each paste is one step: one Ctrl+Z takes it all away.
  • The clipboard stays when another project is opened, so elements can be pasted from one project to another. Their types come along; where that project already has a type with the same name, that one is used. Levels are found by name, then by elevation.
  • Pasted on another level, an element whose top is tied to a level is tied to the level as many levels higher; where there is no such level, it gets a Free Height of the same value.
  • The elements of a view are pasted only into views of the same kind; the model elements are left out of Paste in the chosen views, the elements of a view out of Paste on the chosen levels. The message says how many were left out, and why.
  • A door or window pasted alone goes into the wall it lands on; where there is none, it is left out and the message says so.
  • A copy of a group is copied with its members (see Groups).
  • Paste in the active view is greyed in the view the elements were copied from: there it would not move them. Open another view, or use Paste in the same place.
  • Copied alone, a copy of a model group follows the cursor by its origin.

docs.title: Edit pasted
docs.text:
After every paste, Edit pasted opens: a bar over the drawing with the number of elements pasted, while the rest of the project is in halftone and cannot be selected. The pasted elements can still be moved and changed with the usual tools.

Button What it does Finish selected The selected pasted elements stay where they are and leave the edit Select all Selects all the pasted elements Finish The pasted elements stay: the paste and the changes made to them are a single Ctrl+Z step Cancel The pasted elements go, as before the paste

When a paste left elements out (a door that finds no wall, for example), the message says so and points to the bar.

docs.title: Transfer type
docs.text:
Transfer type (MA), in the same group, gives the type of one element to others. Click the element whose type to take: the brush next to the cursor takes colour, and the status bar names the type. Then click each element that should take it; only elements of the same category change. To give it to many at once, drag a window around them and click Finish selection in the options bar.

Between two walls, besides the type, the base offset, the layer extensions and, when both have one, the unconnected height go across; when they stand on the same base level, also the top constraint and its offset. The other instance parameters stay as they are.

A click on nothing, or Esc, empties the brush to take another type; Esc again ends the tool.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A group keeps elements together as one, and places copies of them elsewhere: every copy of a group is the same, and a change made to one reaches the others.

Group (GP) makes a new group of the selection and its first copy. Doors and windows join with their walls. What the group is depends on what is selected:

  • model elements only: a model group;
  • elements of a view only (lines, texts, dimensions…): a 2D group, which belongs to that view;
  • both: a model group, with an attached 2D group (Attached 2D group) that goes with it.

An element is in one group at most: groups inside groups are not made. Moved, rotated, mirrored or deleted, a copy of a group takes its members with it; copied, it makes a new copy of the same group.

Place group places a new copy of a group at the point clicked, on the active level. Placed on another level, the copy moves its levels up by as many levels: an element whose top is beyond the last level gets a Free Height of the same value. A 2D group is placed in a view.

Edit group opens the group editor on the selected copy: Add and Remove add elements to the group and take members out of it (a wall leaves with its doors and windows; a member removed becomes an ordinary element), Finish ends the edit and every other copy of the group is made again from this one, Cancel leaves the group as it was.

Ungroup turns the members of the selected copy back into ordinary elements; the group stays in the project, with its other copies.

Exclude from this copy takes the selected members out of their copy only: the other copies keep them. Restore excluded brings them back into the copy, taken from another copy.

Attached 2D groups shows in the open view, with the selected copy of a model group, an attached 2D group placed with it as it is with another copy (the dimensions of one copy, for example, then measure the walls of this one); it also hides it again.

In the Project Index, the Groups node lists the groups, under Model and 2D. The menu of a group has Place copy, Select all copies, Rename, Duplicate and Delete; a group is deleted only when it has no copies left.

Duplicate gives the new group the next free number ("Group 1" becomes "Group 2"); F2 renames the group you clicked in the index.

Group with nothing selected opens a window with the name and the kind of the group (Model group or 2D group): the group opens empty in the editor, and what you draw or add there joins it. Finish with no members does not make the group.

A double click on a copy, or on one of its members, opens the group editor on that copy, in a plan, a section, an elevation or a 3D view.

Move to project, in the Group panel or in the right-button menu on a member reached with Tab (next to Exclude), takes the member out of its copy and leaves it in the project as an ordinary element; a wall takes its doors and windows with it. The other copies keep it.

Disassociate from model group, on a copy of an attached 2D group with no dimensions or tags, makes it a 2D group of its own (of a new group, when other copies stay attached).

In the Properties of a copy of a model group, Reference Level and Origin Level Offset move the members: a new level takes them up by as many levels, a new offset raises or lowers them by the difference. Members that cannot follow (a hosted element, a wall attached to a floor) stay where they are, and a warning says so.

docs.title: Typed shortcuts
docs.text: Type the letters and press Enter: MV Move, CO Copy, RO Rotate, MM Mirror on Axis, DM Mirror on Line, AR Repeat in Series, OF Offset, AL Align, TR Shorten/Lengthen, SL Split Element, SG Split with Joint, RE Scale, MA Transfer type, GP Group. PN pins and UP unpins the selection, SA selects all its instances visible in the view. Keyboard shortcuts lists them all.

docs.title: Not yet available
docs.text:
• Tab to reach a part of an element: a curtain panel or mullion, a part of a stacked wall;
  • Select All Instances from a type in the Project Index;
  • Group and Associate of Repeat in Series;
  • splitting walls along a horizontal line in elevations and 3D views;
  • groups inside groups, and Load as group.

docs.title: Site plan and terrain
docs.text: The ground the building stands on and the drawings of the lot around it are made with Massing & site ▸ Site and Edit site. They work in floor plans and in the Site plan; a terrain and a building pad are also sketched in 3D views, on the plane of their level.

docs.title: Terrain
docs.text:
A terrain is a solid: a sketched outline (with holes) on a level, shaped by points, with the layers and thickness of its type.

Terrain ▾ has two ways:

Way How it works Create from sketch Sketch mode Create Terrain Boundary, with the shared Draw group (lines, rectangle, polygons, circle, arcs, Pick Lines). Draw a closed loop; a loop inside it is a hole. Finish Edit Mode makes a flat terrain, its top at Height Offset From Level Create from import The dialog Add points from selected layers: the layers of a DWG or DXF imported with heights (3D lines and points) whose points shape the terrain, or Create from points file… (CSV or TXT, its unit chosen in Format)

A file of points gives on each row x, y and z first; names and other columns are skipped, and two points at the same x, y keep the higher z. Beyond the limit of Site settings (20,000 points by default, 10,000–50,000) the points are sampled down to it and a message says how many were kept.

docs.title: Shape editing
docs.text:
A selected terrain shows the group Shape editing:

Tool How it works Add point Click inside the outline. In the options strip: Absolute (the Elevation typed, from the Elevation base: current level, project base point, survey point, internal origin) or Relative to surface (an offset above or below the surface where you click); XYZ snaps take the elevation of a floor's corner or a wall's end, plus Offset from snaps Modify sub elements Click a point: drag it in plan, or type its height above the terrain's original top Add split line Two clicks: a fold of the surface, straight between their elevations Reset shape Removes every point and split line Simplify terrain Keeps a share of the points (1 000 points at 70 % become 700)

The surface is triangulated through the outline and the points; the contours follow at once.

docs.title: Type, layers and contours
docs.text:
The terrain's type has its Structure in the same Type layers dialog as walls and floors: the layer marked Variable takes up the shape, so the bottom stays flat. Contour display (Contour display in the terrain's panel) lists groups of contours: Start, End, Increment, Single value or Multiple values, the line style (primary, secondary, hidden lines, triangulation edges) and a check box to turn a group off. A new project draws primary contours every 5 m and secondary ones every metre; the types Asphalt road, Gravel path and Sidewalk draw none.

The contours are drawn on the terrain in 3D views too, in their line styles, hidden where the building stands in front of them.

In a section the terrain is cut with its layers and their materials' patterns. A Spot Elevation placed on the terrain reads its elevation there.

Visibility and Graphics ▸ Terrain has the subcategories Primary contours, Secondary contours, Hidden lines, Fold lines, Boundary points and Interior points; the last three are off unless turned on.

Site options ▾ ▸ Terrain smooth shading makes every terrain smooth in the shaded styles.

Site options ▾ ▸ Cut void stability: a cut that does not come out whole is tried again with its outline moved a few millimetres along x or y; Excavate says how many cuts were moved.

docs.title: Editing the terrain
docs.text:
Tool How it works Sub-area Sketch a loop on the selected terrain (or click a terrain first). Its Type gives its material; Sub-area offset raises it (a kerb) or sinks it into the host (with its Excavation volume) Divide terrain Click the terrain, then sketch a closed loop inside it or open lines from edge to edge. A sub-area the division cannot keep asks for Delete instances Merge terrains Click the main terrain, then the second: they must share an edge or overlap. Remove points along shared edges is on by default Excavate / Remove excavation With the terrain selected, click a floor, a roof, a building pad or another terrain that crosses it. Individual excavation volume lists each cut Grading Edit graded region asks for an exact copy or only the boundary's points; click a terrain of an earlier phase. It is demolished in the current phase and its copy, new, opens in shape editing. The copy reports Cut, Fill and Net cut/fill

A schedule of Terrains lists the cut and fill, with a grand total.

docs.title: Building pad
docs.text: Building pad sketches a closed loop over a terrain (Create Pad Boundary, with Pick Walls and Slope Arrow). Its top is at Height Offset From Level; the terrain under it is cut or filled to its underside. Its type has a Structure of layers and the low detail fill pattern.

docs.title: Site elements and parking
docs.text: Site element places trees, shrubs, benches, street lamps and hydrants, one at a click (space bar to rotate); Parking places parking spaces (90°, 60°, 45°, parallel, accessible). Both stand on the terrain or sub-area under the click and follow it when it changes. Pick New Host moves them onto another terrain or sub-area; Repeat in Series makes rows of them.

docs.title: Property lines
docs.text:
Property line asks how to create it:

  • Create by sketching: the lines of sketch mode; an open loop warns that its area cannot be computed (finish again to keep it open);
  • Create by entering distances and bearings: the table Property lines, a row per run with Distance, Bearing (as N 45°00'00" E), Type (line or arc), Radius and L/R; Insert, Delete, Up, Down, and Close, which adds the run back to the start. The runs follow true north.

A selected property line shows Edit table. Site options ▾ ▸ Property data sets the Angle display (bearing or degrees) and the units. Property lines show in site plans and 3D views by default; a schedule of Property lines lists their name and area.

docs.title: Contour labels
docs.text: Contour labels: click the start and the end of a line across the contours; each contour it crosses shows its elevation, turned to read from project north. The label's type sets the text and whether only primary contours are labelled.

docs.title: The site plan
docs.text: Every new project has a Site plan; Views ▸ Plan ▾ ▸ Site plan makes another, for the active level: 1:200, cut above the building down to 10 m below the level, oriented to True north. Orientation in its properties turns it back to Project north.

docs.title: Site settings
docs.text: Site options ▾ ▸ Site settings holds the project's contours (for the terrain types that do not set their own), the Section cut material and Poché base elevation of terrain types without layers, the property data and the most points an import keeps.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text: Terrain from face, Link topography and Surrounding context come in a later phase.

docs.title: Structure and foundations
docs.text: The Structure tab (in the BIMopen style: Create ▸ Structure) gathers the elements that carry the building: beams, braces, beam layouts, trusses, structural walls and floors, structural columns, pad footings, strip footings and raft foundations. Beams, braces and the members of trusses are one category, Structural framing; pad footings, strip footings and raft foundations are Structural foundations. The same tools work in plans, sections, elevations and 3D views, where the view allows it.

docs.title: Structural framing types
docs.text:
Beam and brace types are BIMopen parametric sections, like those of structural columns. Section shape picks the shape: Rectangular (concrete or timber), Round, I-shape (also with unequal and sloped flanges), Rectangular hollow section, Circular hollow section, Angular, C-channel (also with a lip) and T-shape. Type Parameters shows only the dimensions of the chosen shape and computes, read-only, the Structural analysis properties: area, paintable perimeter, nominal weight (from the material's density), moments of inertia, elastic and plastic moduli, torsional and warping constants, shear areas and the angle of the principal axes. Section name key keeps the name of the commercial profile.

A new project has reinforced concrete beams, IPE, HEA, HEB and UPN profiles, angles, T-sections, hollow sections and glued laminated timber beams.

docs.title: Beam
docs.text:
Structure ▸ Beam opens the Place beam card. Two clicks make a beam: the ends snap to the centre of structural columns, to the axis of bearing walls, to the ends and the line of other beams and to grid intersections, and the status bar says to what. The options strip has:

Option What it does Placement plane The level of the view, on which the beam is laid Structural usage derives it from the supports: between columns or walls it is a Girder, between girders a Joist, between joists a Purlin; or pick one 3D Snapping The ends snap to structural elements off the work plane: a sloped beam Chain The end of one beam is the start of the next; Esc ends the chain Tag on Placement Every beam is placed with its tag

Multiple ▸ On Grids: click the grids and End (or Enter); on each grid a beam is made for every span between the supports that cross it. A wall standing on the grid gets no beams; beams already there are not doubled.

In a section or an elevation the beam is drawn in the plane of the view, with its ends on the structural elements clicked; in 3D on the level under the cursor, or with 3D Snapping on the element.

docs.title: Beam properties
docs.text:
Group Properties Constraints Reference level, Work Plane, Start level offset and End level offset (a sloped beam), Orientation (Normal, Horizontal), Cross-section rotation Geometric position Start extension/End extension (free ends), Start join cutback/End join cutback (joined ends, steel and timber), yz Justification (Smooth or Independent), y Justification/z Justification with their Offset value, also for start and end Materials and Finishes Structural material Structural Structural usage, Stick symbol location, Start attachment type/End attachment type, Start attachment distance/End attachment distance and reference column (above or below) for each end, Start connection/End connection (Moment frame, Cantilever moment), Camber size, Number of verticals, Beam seated at start/end on a structural wall, Maximum weight, Exact weight, Painted area Dimensions System length, Cut length, Volume, Elevation at top and Elevation at bottom («Varies» on a sloped beam) Structural analysis Start release/End release (Fixed, Pinned, Bending moment, User defined with the six constraints), Analyze As

A selected beam has Reverse Ends and, for each end, Disallow Join.

docs.title: How it is drawn
docs.text:
• Coarse: a line, with the line style of its usage (Styles by Category ▸ Structural framing ▸ Girder, Joist, Purlin…), held back from the columns and beams it joins by the Cut symbol distance. In sections and elevations beams are lines too, with the moment symbols.
  • Medium and Fine: the outline of the section. In a plan whose Discipline is «Structural» the beams covered by a floor are dashed; in an «Architectural» plan they are not shown.
  • In sections the beam is cut with its material's pattern.

docs.title: Joins
docs.text:
A beam stops at the face of the column and of the bearing wall it rests on (never at a non-bearing wall); between beams the join is a tee (the beam that runs through stays whole) or a corner between two beams of the same type in the same plane. Concrete becomes a single mass: the column wins over the beam, floors and walls keep their shape, and a beam under a concrete floor stops at its underside.

Structure ▸ Framing ▸ Beam/Column Joins shows an arrow at each joined end: towards the join, that beam is cut; a click reverses it. The options strip filters by material (Steel, Wood, Precast concrete, Other).

docs.title: Brace
docs.text:
Structure ▸ Brace:

  • in a Framing Elevation (or in a section), two clicks on structural elements, for example the base of a column and a beam;
  • in plan, with Start level, Offset, End level, Offset on the options strip;
  • in 3D, on the points of the elements clicked.

An end laid on a beam stays attached at a Ratio (from 0 to 1) or a Distance along it, from its start or its end: if the beam moves or gets longer, the brace follows it. Structural usage: Vertical bracing, Kicker bracing, Web, Other.

docs.title: Plan symbols and Structural Settings
docs.text:
Structure ▸ Framing ▸ Structural Settings sets, on paper:

  • the Cut symbol distance of braces, beams and trusses, and columns;
  • the Brace symbols: Parallel line (with its offset) or Angled line, Show brace above and Show brace below (also dashed), Kicker brace symbol;
  • the Connection symbols of beams and braces.

The symbols show at the Coarse detail level.

docs.title: Beam layout
docs.text:
Structure ▸ Beam layout fills a bay with parallel beams:

  • Automatic beam layout: one click in a bay closed by beams or bearing walls;
  • Sketch beam layout: the boundary in sketch mode (Create beam layout boundary) with Pick Supports (the boundary stays tied to the beams and walls clicked, and the first gives the direction), Line, Rectangle, Pick Lines and Beam direction. An inner loop is an opening.

Layout rule: Fixed distance, Fixed number, Maximum spacing, Clear spacing; with the first and the last, Justification (Start, End, Center, Direction line). Beam type, Elevation and Tag on Placement (one tag for the layout or one per beam) complete the options.

The beams follow the supports when they move. A selected beam layout has Reset System (beams that were changed go back to the layout) and Remove Beam Layout (the layout goes, the beams stay).

The layout rules space the beams as Array spaces its copies: Fixed number like Last, Fixed distance like 2° from the Justification; with Clear spacing the gap is between the faces, and a beam of a bigger type pushes its neighbours away. 3D in the options bar makes the system non-planar: the beams' ends rise to the slope-defining supports (beams always, walls with Defines Slope or Defined slope walls). Edit Boundary opens the sketch again; Beam direction is drawn or picked with Pick Lines. A beam deleted by hand stays deleted until Reset System. Outside a closed bay, Automatic beam layout opens the boundary sketch.

A beam system copied, mirrored or pasted associates itself with the beams and bearing walls its edges fall on in the new place; when an edge finds no support the command warns, and Edit Boundary ▸ Pick Supports associates it again. Copy it only between bays with the same shape and the same supports.

Curved beams and curved bearing walls also close a bay for an automatic beam system, but the beams' direction always comes from a straight support. A beam system sketched over more than one bay is still made, with a warning: the beams and walls across it do not divide it, so one beam system per bay is better.

docs.title: Truss
docs.text:
Structure ▸ Truss: two clicks in plan lay the type's pattern (Pratt, Howe, Warren, Warren with verticals, Fink) over the span. The chords are beams, the webs are braces, each of the type of its group (Top chords, Vertical webs, Diagonal webs, Bottom chords). The properties include Truss height, Bearing chord, Maximum panel width, Number of panels and the rotation.

A selected truss has Attach Top/Bottom (the chord follows the face of a roof or a structural floor; with Shift the bottom chord), Detach Top/Bottom, Reset Truss and Remove truss (the members stay as beams and braces).

Edit Profile opens a section or elevation parallel to the truss (when the open view is not, Go to View asks which) with the chords' lines in sketch mode: the lines above the middle are the top chord, the others the bottom chord, and the webs follow them. Reset Profile brings the chords back to the layout's line. In a 3D view the lines are drawn straight on the truss's plane, without changing view.

With Pick Lines the truss is placed along a beam, a wall or a grid. A click on a member selects the whole truss; Tab goes on to the single member. An attached chord follows the host's face along the whole span; with the bearing chord attached, the other keeps the Truss height from it, and the drawn profile stays and comes back with Detach Top/Bottom. Bearing vertical justification, Non-bearing offset, Web orientation (Orthogonal: the verticals square to the bearing chord) and Rotation angle (the truss's plane turns about the location line) change the members. A member deleted by hand stays deleted until Reset Truss; the members are cut only in Structural Settings. New layouts drawn in their own component will come with the component editor.

With Webs have cut symbols in the truss type, at coarse detail the webs stop short of the chords by the braces' Cut symbol distance from Structural Settings.

docs.title: Structural wall and structural floor
docs.text:
Structural wall is the Wall tool with the same types and the same options strip: the wall is made Bearing. Every wall has Structural and Structural usage (Non-bearing, Bearing, Shear wall, Structural combined).

Structural floor is the floor with Structural ticked. In the sketch, Span direction draws the direction of its span; at the end the Span direction symbol is placed at the centre of the floor. Annotations ▸ Span direction places it again (with Automatic placement at the centre); selected, it can be turned, and Align perpendicular makes it perpendicular to an edge, a beam or a grid.

docs.title: Shape editing
docs.text:
A selected floor (structural, a slab foundation or any floor) has the Shape Editing panel:

  • Modify Sub Elements: click a corner or a point, then type its Elevation in the options bar; Del removes the point.
  • Add Point: a point inside the floor at the elevation given; with Relative it is added to the surface's height there.
  • Add Split Line: two clicks; the surface creases along the line.
  • Pick Supports: click a beam under the floor; a split line follows the beam, at its top.
  • Reset Shape: removes the points and lines; the floor is flat again (or keeps its slope).

The top becomes the triangulated surface through these points; the whole slab follows it and keeps its thickness. Elevation at Top and Elevation at Bottom then show Varies.

docs.title: Foundations
docs.text:
Tool How it works Pad footing One click in plan or in 3D (space bar: turn), or At Grids or At Columns and End. The top face is at the level plus Height Offset From Level; the column above rests on the footing. Moves with grids ties it to the grids Strip footing One click on a structural wall: the footing runs under its base and follows it. Bearing: Width and Eccentricity; Retaining: Outer side width and Inner side width. It breaks under doors and windows that touch the base, unless Do not break at inserts; at free ends it projects by the Default end extension length Raft foundation The boundary in sketch mode (Create raft boundary), like a floor: it lies under its level, down by the thickness of its layers. Structural usage: Foundation or Foundation slab

With a wall foundation selected, the filled circles at its ends lengthen or shorten it along the wall, snapping to what is near; the circles at the ends of a beam or a brace do the same. On steel, precast concrete and timber beams, the arrows beyond the ends change Start/End extension at a free end and Start/End join cutback at a joined one. Concrete pads and wall foundations that touch are one mass: the pad keeps its shape and cuts the wall foundation (of two pads, the earlier cuts the other), and no line is drawn between them in plan.

docs.title: Rebar cover
docs.text: Reinforced concrete ▸ Cover options lists the project's covers, each with a name and a distance: Add, Duplicate, Delete. Elements that used a deleted cover take the first one. Structural walls, pillars, concrete beams and braces, structural floors, slab foundations, isolated and wall foundations choose their cover in Properties: Rebar cover - Top face, Rebar cover - Bottom face and Rebar cover - Other faces (on walls Rebar cover - Exterior face, Rebar cover - Interior face and Rebar cover - Other faces).

docs.title: Views, tags, schedules and IFC
docs.text:
• A view's Discipline: Architectural or Structural. The second hides non-bearing walls and dashes what floors cover.
  • Annotations ▸ Beam tags: framing tags and elevations on all the beams of the plan (or on the selected ones) in six positions, above and below, at the start, the middle and the end; Display elevation picks top, bottom, both or actual.
  • A beam's tag reads along the beam and stands beside it, on the side where it covers no other beam (above, when both are free); it is dragged like any tag. In Beam tags ▸ Settings, Horizontal end offset moves the start and end positions towards the middle and Vertical offset keeps the annotations away from the beam's side.
  • Schedule/Quantities has the categories Structural framing, Beam layouts, Trusses and Structural foundations, with every parameter as a field.
  • In IFC girders, joists and purlins are exported as IfcBeam, braces and members as IfcMember, trusses as IfcElementAssembly, pad and strip footings as IfcFooting, the raft as a base IfcSlab; structural walls and floors carry LoadBearing.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: This chapter collects situations that can surprise you, and what to do about them. It grows with the manual: each area of the realignment adds its own.

docs.title: The web app shows «BIMopen non si è avviato» and an error
docs.text:
The browser could not give BIMopen a graphics surface: the message ends with webgl2 not available or with a WebGPU error. BIMopen in the browser needs WebGPU or WebGL2.

  • Turn on hardware acceleration in the settings of the browser, then reload the page.
  • Try another browser, or a newer version of the same one.
  • Add ?webgl to the address to use WebGL2 even where WebGPU exists but does not work.

docs.title: The desktop app does not build on Linux
docs.text:
The interface needs the development files of xkbcommon, Wayland and GTK 3. On Debian and Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get install -y libxkbcommon-dev libwayland-dev libgtk-3-dev

docs.title: The element panel or the Project Index has disappeared
docs.text: Views ▸ Windows ▸ Panels shows or hides them: tick them again there. The Properties tile of the contextual card also shows the element panel again. A click on the rail entry already chosen folds the tool panel: click it again to open it.

docs.title: What I type ends up at the command line
docs.text: Whatever you type while no field is being edited goes to the command line, the search box of the top bar: this is how typed shortcuts work. To type in a field of the element panel or of a dialog, click the field first.

docs.title: A tile is greyed
docs.text: Some tools work only in the right view, and their tip says why. Area Outline and Area need an open area plan: the tip says Open an area plan first. Save View needs an open 3D view; Document ▸ Sheets ▸ View needs an open sheet; Undo and Redo are greyed when there is nothing to undo or redo.

docs.title: DL starts a dimension instead of a detail line
docs.text: DL is the short form of the linear dimension. To draw detail lines, use Document ▸ Detail ▸ Detail line, or type detailline.

docs.title: «no wall at that point»
docs.text: A door or a window must be placed in a wall. Click on the wall itself, or give a point on its line at the command line.

docs.title: A height set at the command line is enormous
docs.text: At the command line a number without unit is in metres: set Free Height 2700 makes the wall 2700 m high. Undo with Ctrl+Z and write the unit: 2700mm or 2.7m. In the element panel a number without unit is in the project's units.

docs.title: Unsaved work is gone after New, Open or Sample project
docs.text: These commands replace the current project without asking. Save before using them: the asterisk Unsaved changes in the top bar shows that there are changes to save.

docs.title: Open… in the browser does not show a file dialog
docs.text: In the browser, drag the .bpr file into the page: the command line says Drag a .bpr file into the window to open it.

docs.title: bimopen-cli prints its usage and stops
docs.text: The arguments are not the ones it expects: it ends with code 2 and shows the usage. A command that fails ends with code 1 and a message saying which line failed. See Command line and MCP.

docs.title: Views and graphics
docs.text: This chapter describes the views of the model, how each one is drawn, and how to change what a view shows and how: graphic styles, scale and detail, the cut heights of a plan, crop regions, hiding and isolating, Visibility and Graphics, filters and view templates. Line weights, line patterns and styles by category are described in the same terms by the program's dialogs of Settings on the rail.

docs.title: 3D views
docs.text:
Views ▸ Create ▸ 3D View ▸ Default 3D View opens the default 3D view, {3D}, framing the whole model; opened again, it shows the model as it was left. Drag to orbit (or Shift and the middle button), drag with the middle button to pan, and turn the wheel to zoom at the cursor; see The interface.

The default 3D view, {3D}

To keep a framing, Views ▸ Create ▸ 3D View ▸ Save View: type a name and press Enter. The new view is listed under 3D Views in the Project Index and opens at once; it keeps the framing it is left with. Renaming {3D} in the Project Index (right-click ▸ Rename…) does the same: {3D} becomes a named view, and the next default 3D view is a new {3D}.

A selected element is washed in blue and half see-through, its edges in blue: what is behind it stays visible.

Floors cut the walls they pass through: where a slab crosses a wall the wall stops under it and goes on above it, so the slab's edge and the wall's face are one surface.

docs.title: Section box, projection and orientation
docs.text:
{3D} starts orthographic, looking from the south-east corner. Right-click the orientation cube: Prospettica or Ortogonale, Vai all'inizio, Salva vista…, Blocca selezione (the orbit turns about the chosen elements), Ripristina Fronte, Orienta su direzione (the compass points and Alto), Orienta su vista (a plan, section or elevation: the view takes its viewpoint and a section box reproduces its extents) and Orienta su piano… (a level, a grid or a reference plane).

In the 3D view's Properties, Estensioni ▸ Riquadro di sezione switches the section box on: the first time it wraps the visible model. Outside the box the model is not shown and the parts it cuts are closed on its faces, layer by layer. A click on an edge selects the box: the six arrows move a face, the circle above turns it. Each change is one undo step; switched off, the box keeps its size. In the Project Browser, right-click a 3D view ▸ Mostra riquadro di sezione shows it in plans and sections too, with grips. Visibilità e grafica ▸ Riquadri di sezione hides its drawing, not the cut.

The section box cuts the model at the ground floor

With Sezione the options bar offers Tipo (Sezione edificio, Sezione di muro, Dettaglio) and Scala vista; the Browser lists the view under its type's branch. Prospetto is placed with one click beside a wall: the symbol looks at it (Tab turns it). Right-click Viste in the Browser ▸ Organizzazione del browser… chooses how the views are listed: by type, discipline, phase, level, only those not on sheets, or an organisation of your own.

The cut faces show the material's cut pattern; at Basso detail they show the Materiale poché a dettaglio basso chosen in Properties (: each part's own material). With the box selected, EH hides its drawing in the view; BX puts the box around the selected elements. {3D} and the saved 3D views have Ritaglia vista and Regione di taglio visibile too: the image is limited to the rectangle, dragged by its sides. Orienta su piano… also takes a click on a face (Seleziona un piano) or on a line (its work plane).

Sezione is drawn in a section, an elevation or a detail too: it is made across that view. Rif. ad altra vista makes the section open an existing view (or a new free 2D view) instead of its own; Offset moves the line sideways. With an elevation placed by one click selected, its symbol shows four boxes: a click switches the elevation towards that side on or off (interior elevations), the outer grip turns the symbol. In the Browser, Ctrl and Shift pick several views: Applica modello vista…, Duplica and Elimina act on them all.

docs.title: Perspective views
docs.text:
Views ▸ Create ▸ 3D View ▸ Perspective view puts a camera in a plan, a section or an elevation. The options bar (in the BIMopen style, the tool panel) has the Level and the Offset, the eyes' height above the level (1.60 m, as in walk mode); Perspective is always on. The first click is where the camera stands; the triangle of what it sees follows the cursor, and the second click is the point it looks at, at the same height. 3D View 1 (then 2, 3…) is made under 3D Views in the Project Index and opens beside the plan, cropped. In a section or an elevation the two clicks give the heights too.

The view is drawn in its crop region, in its proportions (240 × 160 mm on paper); what lies beyond the far clip plane (at first, as far as the point looked at) is not drawn. Its properties, in the Extents and Camera groups: Crop View, Crop Region Visible, Far clip plane and its distance, Reference level, Eye elevation and Target elevation (from the level), Field of view.

Right-click the view in the Project Index ▸ Show camera selects the camera in the plans, sections and elevations (so does a click on the crop region's border in the 3D view). Drag its body to move it (with Shift the target stays), the red point to turn it, the triangle's corners for the field of view and the square on its base for the far clip plane; in an elevation or a section you change the heights. The 3D view follows while you drag, and each drag is undone with Ctrl+Z. On the Modify | Cameras tab: Reset target puts the target on the model seen at the middle of the crop region, Size Crop changes the width and height on paper by Field of view (more is seen) or Scale (locked proportions), Reset crop (240 × 160 mm, 50°), Open the view. Dragging the crop region's sides in the 3D view changes the field of view too.

The live view of a camera view follows it, walk mode starts at its eye and, when you leave, the camera stays where you walked to; a New path starts at its pose. From the command line: camera {"from":[14,-6],"to":[5,3]} makes the view, camera {"eye":[15,-6,1.6],"fov":60,"far":20} changes it, camera {"reset_target":true} resets the target.

docs.title: Graphic styles
docs.text:
The Graphic Style button of the view control bar, at the bottom of every view window, offers:

Style What is drawn Wireframe Every edge, also those behind other faces; no faces Lines Faces as paper and the edges in front of them in ink; on the dark background paper and lines are inverted together Shaded Faces lit, in the colour of their material Shaded with Edges As Shaded, with the edges in front Flat Colors Faces in the colour of their material, the same whatever the light Realistic Faces as in a photograph: the light of the project’s sun and sky, reflections, ambient shadows, see-through glass, haze Pastel A watercolour drawing: faces washed in their material's colour, close to the paper in the sun, deeper in shade; the lines drawn by hand Wireframe, Lines and Shaded with Edges

The style belongs to the view and can be undone. The keyboard shortcuts WF, HL and SD choose Wireframe, Lines and Shaded.

The edges are the real ones: where two faces meet at an angle, and the outline of each face and each opening. A wall with a window shows its own outline and the window's, and no line where the pieces of the wall meet.

Plans, sections and elevations have a graphic style too. A plan is drawn in Lines until another style is chosen. In Lines the surfaces, cut or seen, are not coloured: what is cut shows its material's cut pattern; at Coarse detail the type's coarse fill pattern, or else only its outline. In Shaded, Shaded with Edges and Flat Colors every element seen or cut is filled with the shading colour of its material (a part with no material takes its category's, from Styles by Category, else the category's default colour; the 3D view follows the same rule): walls (each layer where it is cut), floors, roofs, doors, windows, furniture and components, stairs and railings. Plans are flat; in sections and elevations Shaded darkens a little the faces turned away from the viewer, such as the slopes of a roof, while Flat Colors keeps them all alike. At Medium and Fine detail the cut patterns stay on top of the colour. Sheets, prints and exported drawings show the views as the screen does.

A plan in Lines and in Shaded

The rooms' colour scheme shows in every style. With Color scheme location at Background it lies under the model's lines: in a plan over the floors and under the furniture, in a section over the surfaces seen through each room it cuts. At Foreground it covers the model, under the annotations.

docs.title: Realistic style
docs.text:
Realistic draws the 3D view like a photograph, in real time, and the view stays editable as in the other styles.

Realistic at night: moon and stars
  • Light of the sun and the sky. The light is that of the project’s sun (place, date and time in Sun settings) and of the sky that sun gives: blue by day, warmer and darker at sunset. The sun lights the model even with shadows off; with Cast shadows its shadows are those of the other styles. What is in shadow stays lit by the sky and the ground. The sun's disc appears when it comes into the frame, with a glow, and the model hides it. Towards sunset the sun's light turns warm and weaker and the shadows lengthen; after sunset only the sky is left, fading into a blue-violet twilight with a pink band on the horizon on the sun's side; at night the sky is dark blue and the scene almost dark (self-illuminated surfaces stay visible). Dragging the sun or following a sun study changes the light continuously.
  • Moon and stars. The moon is where it is at the project's place, date and time, in its phase: lit on the side facing the sun, the rest faintly grey (earthshine), redder near the horizon. At night it is the light: with Cast shadows the model casts moonlight shadows, and a full moon lights the scene softly where a new moon leaves it almost dark. Once the sun is down the brighter stars come out in their places, more of them the darker the sky.
  • Materials. Surfaces take the look of their material (the Appearance tab of Materials): the texture image at its real size, the roughness and its map, the relief, metal, glass and water, self-illumination (seen, not lighting others). A material without a look of its own derives it from its colour and transparency; a part without a material takes its category’s colour. On the web the images arrive later: until then the colour shows. The preview of the Appearance tab shows the material on a sphere, a cube or a 2 × 2 m wall.
  • Glass. Glass shows what is behind it and reflects the sky and the sun, more when seen at a grazing angle. Panes are drawn from the farthest to the nearest.
  • Ambient shadows. With Show Ambient Shadows corners and recesses, which get less light from the sky, are darker.
  • Haze. In the distance the air veils the model: Distance haze sets how much, and how clear the sky is.
  • Exposure. Automatic follows the light of the scene and adapts in about half a second when it changes (turning the camera from the sky to the shade, or changing the time). Manual uses the Value (EV): higher is darker, about 15 under the midday sun.

In the Realistic group of the Graphic display options: Exposure and Value (EV), White point (the light shown as white: 6500 K is daylight as it is, a lower value cools the image, a higher one warms it), Saturation, Highlights and Shadows (lower or raise the lightest and darkest tones) and Distance haze. Show Edges draws the edges over the faces. The lighting Scheme is for now always Exterior: sun. Sun, Ambient light and Shadow intensity set the sun’s light, the sky’s and how dark the sun’s shadows are.

The Physical sky (time and place) Background shows behind the model the same sky that lights it, with the sun’s disc; with None, Sky or Gradient the background stays as chosen and the sky still lights the model. Switching to Realistic, a view whose background is None gets Physical sky (time and place), and goes back to None on changing to another style. Selected elements and the sun path look as in the other styles.

On the web without WebGPU (with WebGL2) Realistic works without ambient shadows, and the automatic exposure is set from the sky instead of from the image. On the web and on Android, while the camera moves, the view may be drawn smaller to stay smooth, and turns sharp again when it stops. Without a graphics card Realistic is shown as Shaded and the status bar says so. Plans, sections and elevations in Realistic are for now drawn as in Shaded; sheets, prints and exported images do not show Realistic yet.

docs.title: Pastel style
docs.text:
The Pastel style draws the view as a watercolour or marker drawing: each face is a uniform wash of its material's colour, softly graded, never striped. Faces in the sun stay close to the paper; faces turned from the sun take the same colour, deeper and cooler, never grey; where a cast shadow falls the wash goes deeper still, with a clear edge. Glass is a blue-grey wash with a warm glint. The wash fades towards the edges of the drawing, so the paper shows round the model; the paper has a barely visible grain. Choosing Pastel turns the Sketchy lines on, in ink; they can be turned off, and they go off when the view changes to another style.

It applies to every view. In 3D views the light is that of Realistic: the project's sun and its shadows. In plans, sections and elevations the paper is cream, the faces and floors are washed in their materials' colours and the cut parts are a solid, dark poché in their material's tone. The cast shadows are the view's own: they are turned on, off, deeper or fainter with the same settings as in the other styles (Shadow Intensity), in a clear, dark warm tone. Printing and export come out washed as on screen, 3D views too.

Pastel is the same whatever the window's background: always its light paper, with the same washes, poché and shadows.

The Pastel group of the Graphic Display Options is set per view and view templates carry it: Wash Strength (how deep the colour is laid), Wash Variation (how unevenly it lies on a face), Paper Grain and Saturation (how much of the materials' colours the wash keeps), from 0 to 100, and Paper Colour (with Chosen a colour of its own; without, the warm white paper). From the command line: graphicoptions {"style":"Pastello","pastel_density":70,"paper_color":"auto"}.

Pastel: wash 70, variation 55, grain 40, saturation 75 (the defaults) Section A in Pastel, with the default values

docs.title: Live view and walk mode
docs.text:
Live View (View tab ▸ Presentation, or the button of the 3D view's floating bar) opens a window beside the 3D view that draws it in the Realistic style, with the sun's shadows and the physical sky, and follows its camera: orbit or zoom the 3D view and the live view looks from the same place; every change to the model shows at once. While the camera moves the live view draws a draft, then refines. At the bottom of the live view, Time sets the hour of the view's own sun (sunrise and sunset are marked on the slider); Project Sun goes back to the project's shared sun. The view's properties have the group Live View: Follows the 3D View and Draft While Moving. From the command line: liveview 3d {"follows":true,"draft":true}.

Walk (View tab ▸ Presentation, the 3D view's floating bar, the Classic style's navigation bar or the command search) is a command like the others: the Modify | Walk contextual tab opens, the Options Bar shows its choices and the status bar says what to do. The active 3D view becomes the eyes of someone walking through the model: you stand on the floor under the middle of the view, facing where the view looked. The pointer is captured at the first click in the view (until then the tab and the Options Bar can still be used):

Key W A S D or the arrows walk the mouse look around Shift run comma and full stop, or the wheel slower and faster F Walk or Fly E and Q, Page Up and Page Down rise and sink (flying) K a keyframe R start and stop recording Esc leave walk mode

The other shortcuts wait until you leave. Walking, gravity keeps you on floors, landings and slabs; a step a little higher than the project's highest riser is climbed without noticing, so stairs and ramps are climbed by walking; walls, columns, railings, furniture and window glass stop you, and you slide along them; doors are walked through. Fly drops gravity and collisions. You leave with Esc, Modify, Leave in the tab or by choosing another command; the view stays where you got to. A plan of the level you are on shows where you are and what you see.

The Modify | Walk tab has Mode (Walk, Fly), Walkthrough (Keyframe, Record) and Walk (Options…, Leave); in the BIMopen style they are in the tool panel's tab. The Options Bar has Walk or Fly, the eye height, the speed, Walkthrough (where keyframes and the recording go: New or one of the project's walkthroughs), Move parallel to the ground, Turn sensitivity and Inertia (the gaze starts and stops smoothly; 0 % as before). While walking, the Properties palette shows the walking speed, running, the flying speed, the eye height, gravity and collisions, the step climbed, the sensitivity and the inertia, Invert vertical axis, Record into, Keyframe every and the smoothness of the recorded walkthrough. On a touch screen a joystick walks, a drag on the view looks, and buttons run, fly, rise and sink, set keyframes, record and leave.

Options… opens the Walk Mode settings. Movement holds the personal choices, the same in every project: eye height (1.60 m), walking speed, running, flying speed, Turn sensitivity, Turn inertia, Keyframe every, Invert vertical axis, field of view and Fly parallel to the ground. Collisions by category holds the project's: for each group of categories whether Disable Collision is on (it is for doors and curtain wall door panels), and the Step height, taken from the stairs unless you type it. From the command line: walksettings {"step":0.22}, collision {"group":"furniture","off":true}.

docs.title: Disable Collision
docs.text: Every element with a body has Disable Collision in the Walk Mode group of its properties: on, whoever walks passes through it. Its value comes from the type, and the type's from its category; Collision From Type (on a type, Collision From Category) says so, and setting Disable Collision makes the value the element's own. Several elements selected show ‹varies› where they differ. Schedules can list it as a field and filters can use it as a rule. It changes nothing but walk mode. A floor, stair or ramp with collision disabled carries no one either. From the command line: collision 42 {"off":true}, or {"off":null} to take the type's value again.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
Walkthrough (View tab ▸ 3D View ▾, or the command search) is drawn in a plan, a section or an elevation like a wall: the Options Bar has Perspective, the Level and the Offset (1.60 m, the walk's eyes); each click sets a keyframe and the next stretch follows the cursor, with the camera's triangle at the start. In a section or an elevation the clicks give the height too. A double click, Esc or Finish walkthrough in the tab end the path (Cancel walkthrough drops it): Walkthrough 1 is made, in the Walkthroughs branch of the Project Browser, and opens beside, at frame 1. It is a camera view that moves: it has its crop region, its far clip plane and the camera's properties, plus Walkthrough frames and Frame.

Selected in a plan (a click on the path, or Show Camera in the Project Browser), the walkthrough is edited in the Modify Walkthrough tab. Controls in the Options Bar chooses what the grips do:

  • Active camera: the camera is dragged along the path, snapping to the keyframes; on a keyframe the red point says where it looks and is dragged, and the triangle's corners change the field of view;
  • Path: the keyframes become grips; in a section or an elevation their height changes;
  • Add keyframe: a click on the path adds one;
  • Delete keyframe: a click on one removes it (at least two stay).

Frame shows the view's frame and can be typed; beside it the previous keyframe, previous frame, next frame and next keyframe buttons and Play, which plays the walkthrough in its view from the frame shown to the last; the status bar says "frame 87 of 300", with Cancel; Esc stops. Reset cameras makes every keyframe look along the path again.

Frames… opens Walkthrough frames: Total frames (300), Frames per second (15), Total time (20 s), Uniform speed (on: the camera always goes at the same speed; off, each keyframe has its Acceleration, from 0.1 to 10, for the stretch starting there), and for each keyframe its frame, speed and elapsed time. Turn smoothness says how the gaze turns where the path changes direction: 0 % at once on the keyframe, 100 % along half the stretch before and half after, starting and stopping smoothly; the path has one and each keyframe may have its own. The graph below shows the turn of the gaze over time. Indicators with Frame increment marks the frames along the path in plan.

Export… (also in File ▸ Export ▸ Images and Animations ▸ Walkthrough…) opens Length/Format: All frames or a Frame range from–to, Frames per second (the total time follows), the Graphic style (the view's or another), Size and Zoom, then the file type: an AVI film (Motion-JPEG), with the images too if wanted, or a sequence of JPEG, PNG, TIFF or BMP images. A bar shows the progress, with Cancel.

While walking, Keyframe (K) adds a keyframe where you stand, looking where you look, to the walkthrough chosen in the Options Bar; with New the second makes Walkthrough N. Record (R) makes a walkthrough of the walk: a keyframe every second (Keyframe every), as long as the walk lasted and as smooth as the Inertia. The paths of projects saved before become Walkthrough views when opened. From the command line: walkthrough {"points":[[0,-6],[5,-6],[5,2]],"offset":1.6}, walkthrough 42 {"frame":"next_key"}, walkthrough 42 {"frames":150,"uniform":false,"key":{"index":0,"accel":2}}; walk {"from":[4,2.5],"to":[8,2.5]} shows where a walk ends.

docs.title: Sun and shadows
docs.text:
Plans, sections, elevations and 3D views show the sun (drafting views, legends, sheets and schedules do not). The view control bar has two buttons, each with a small arrow for its menu (the right button opens it too):

  • Sun Path: its menu has Show Sun Path / Hide Sun Path, Sun Settings… and Fit to Model (frames the whole sun path);
  • Shadows: its menu has Shadows On / Shadows Off, Graphic Display Options… and Preview Sun Study.

While either is on, the bar also shows the sun's hour and date, each with − and + (a quarter of an hour, a day). The same buttons and menus are in the Sun and shadows menu of the BIMopen style's view bar, in the touch mode's view sheet and in the view's context menu. Sun Path is also a check box of the view's Properties (Graphics), with Sun Path Size (100–500 %, 150 % by default) and Shared Sun.

Shadows are computed from the model and the sun, the same in every view: in plans they fall on what the plan shows and, where nothing stands, on the plane of a level (Ground Plane at Level in the sun settings, otherwise on the ground, the lowest level); in sections and elevations they fall on the façades and on what is behind them, from eaves, balconies, recesses and other buildings, and so in 3D views. In Lines (hidden line) a shadow is a grey of the paper, in the shaded styles it darkens the materials' colours. Faces cut by the view stay in the light.

The sun path is a ring round the model with the points of the compass at true north, the day's arc with its hours, the analemma (where the sun stands at that hour through the year: one smooth figure of eight, every day at the clock of the chosen date), the part a study goes through, and the sun with its hour and date; in a 3D view it is a dome over the ring. In plans, sections, elevations and 3D views the sun can be dragged: along the day it snaps to quarters of an hour, along the year it follows the analemma day by day (across a change of summer time the clock moves by the change, so the sun does not jump); Shift while dragging takes the other, and Along the Day / Along the Year in the sun path's menu choose which comes first. The shadows follow the drag: in plans, sections and elevations, while the sun moves, they are a coarser draft, each view showing its last shadows until the new ones are ready, and they are drawn in full when the sun is released. With the view under the cursor (and nothing selected, or after a click on the sun), Left and Right move the hour, Up and Down the date. With Lighting the sun stands still and has no path.

The sun path and shadows in the 3D view

The sun path's menu (in the view bar, in the view's menu and in touch mode) also has Visual Aids that help read it: Vertical Hour Lines (from each even hour a dashed line down to the ground and out to the ring, with the hour there; in plans a dot on the ring), Arc Projected on the Ground, Solar Noon (the arc's highest point with its clock time, and the north–south line), Band of the Year (the sky the sun crosses in the year, in a light yellow, the arcs of the solstices and of the equinox, the analemmas of the even hours), Sunrise and Sunset (marks on the ring with their times; the view bar shows them with the length of the day) and Analemma; all but the projection are on at first. In a 3D view what stands behind the model is hidden by it. Sun Settings also show the year's sunrises and sunsets as a chart: a click or a drag on it picks the day.

Shared Sun: the views share the project's sun unless they have one of their own (the Shared Sun property). Moving the shared sun in one view moves it in every view that shares it; a view with its own sun is not touched. Shared Sun in All Views in the sun settings puts every view back on it.

Each change is one step of Undo; the sun command does the same at the command line and over MCP (see Command line and MCP).

docs.title: Sun settings
docs.text:
Sun Settings… opens a dialog with the sun's azimuth, altitude, time and date in its header:

  • on the left the presets: one unsaved row for each mode, the built-in ones (Summer Solstice, Winter Solstice, Spring Equinox, Autumn Equinox, Summer, from 9 to 17, Light from top right) and the project's own; Save…, Duplicate…, Rename… and Delete (only the project's presets are renamed or deleted);
  • in the middle the mode and its fields:
Mode What it takes Still the Date and the Time; Shared Sun in All Views One Day the Date, From Sunrise to Sunset or a Start Time and an End Time, the Frame Interval (15, 30 or 45 minutes, 1 hour); the number of Frames follows Multi-Day From and To (day/month), the Time, the Interval (1 hour, 1 day, 1 week, 1 month) Lighting Azimuth (°) and Altitude (°); Relative to View: the light follows the view's direction

Then the project's Location (a city, or Custom with its latitude and longitude: one for the whole project; a custom place takes the time zone of the nearest city; a new project starts in Rome, the sample house stands in Cagliari) with Daylight Saving Time, which is automatic: the place's rule (Europe, North America, Chile, South-eastern Australia, New Zealand, Egypt, or none) and the exact Sunday of the sun's Year, so the times on the sun path and in the studies are those of the clock; the rule can be changed. Then Ground Plane at Level with its Ground Level; - on the right the preview: the sky seen from above, with the day's path, the analemma and the sun. Preview in the dialog's header, right of the figures, is a switch that hides and shows it; the dialog keeps its size, and without the preview the settings take its room.

Apply changes the view's sun and keeps the dialog open, OK changes it and closes it, Cancel changes nothing. Projects made before the project had a location keep each view's place and date: the first view whose sun was changed gives the project its location, and the views whose sun was changed keep theirs as their own.

Sun Settings

docs.title: Sun study
docs.text: Preview Sun Study (in the Shadows menu) shows the study bar over the view: ⏮ −10, ⏴, ⏵ Play / ⏸ Pause, ⏵, +10 ⏭ and frame n of N. A sun of one moment is studied through its day. Save as Image saves the frame shown as a PNG named after the view, the date and the hour; Export Study… saves every frame as a PNG or JPEG image sequence (a film needs a video encoder BIMopen does not have: the choice is greyed, with the reason). × closes the bar; another view closes it too.

docs.title: Graphic display options
docs.text:
