Graphic Display Options… sets the graphic options of the active view, in groups that open and close with a click on their title (the window remembers which are open, and keeps its size and place):

  • Model Display: the Graphic Style; Show Edges (the edges over the faces in the Shaded, Consistent Colors and Realistic styles; ticked and grey in the styles that always draw them); Smooth Lines with Anti-Aliasing (the 3D view's lines and edges smoothed; without, sharper and faster to draw; plans, sections and elevations always have smooth lines); Transparency (0–100: every face of the view turns see-through and what lies behind shows, in the Hidden Line style the hidden edges too; it applies to 3D views in the styles with faces, to Realistic in a next phase); Silhouette Edges (None, Medium, Thick: a thicker line round the model's outline).
  • Shadows: Cast Shadows and Show Ambient Shadows (corners and recesses darkened).
  • Sketchy Lines: see Sketchy lines.
  • Depth Cueing (sections and elevations): with Show Depth what is farther from the view's line fades into the background. Fade Start and Fade End (as a percentage of the view's depth) set where it starts and ends; Fade Limit how much of what is farthest stays visible (0: it vanishes, 100: no fading). Lines, faces, patterns and sketchy lines fade, on screen as in print and export, on the light and on the dark background; annotations and cut parts stay as they are.
  • Lighting: the Scheme (for now always Exterior: sun), the Sun Settings (the button opens them), Artificial Lights… (grey: they come in a next phase), Sun, Ambient Light and Shadow Intensity (0–100).
  • Realistic: the settings of the Realistic style (see Realistic style).
  • Pastel: the settings of the Pastel style (see Pastel style).
  • Background (3D views): None, Sky, Gradient, Physical sky (time and place); with Gradient, Sky Color, Horizon Color and Ground Color, from the top down. Image is grey: it comes in a next phase.

At the bottom, Save as View Template… applies the options to the view and asks for the name of a new view template that carries them. Every numeric setting has its slider and a field to type the value. The preview draws the view with the options chosen; the Preview switch in the header hides and shows it, as in the sun settings. In the Realistic style the preview looks as the view does. View templates carry these options with the graphic style, and the sun and the shadows as Sun and shadows. On the command line: graphicoptions {"edges":true,"transparency":30,"depth":true,"depth_limit":20,"background":"sfumatura","sky_color":"189-209-208"}.

Graphic Display Options, with the default values Transparency at 60%: the faces are see-through; the default is 0 Gradient background, with the default colours Depth Cueing: start 0%, end 25%, limit 10%

docs.title: Sketchy lines
docs.text:
The Sketchy Lines group of Graphic Display Options… draws the view's lines as by hand. Enable Sketchy Lines turns it on for the active view; Distortion (0–10) sets how much each line wavers and how many times it is traced over (0 straight, twice from 4, three times from 8); long lines waver more than short ones. Extension (0–10) sets how far the lines run past their ends, past the corners where they meet (0 stops them there). They start at 5 and 1 in plans, sections, elevations and 2D views, at 8 and 3 in 3D views. The ✎ button of the view bar (in every interface style; in touch mode, in the view's sheet) turns them on and off for the active view: Enable Sketchy Lines / Disable Sketchy Lines.

They apply in every view (plans, sections, elevations, drafting views, 3D views, views on sheets) and in every visual style: to the lines of the model, of detail items and of fill patterns. Annotations stay straight: dimensions, text, levels, grids, reference planes, tags, symbols and view marks. A view draws the same lines at every redraw and after orbiting back, and prints and exports exactly as the window shows it: PDF and SVG keep the lines as vectors, a printed section or elevation leaves out only the parts nearer surfaces hide. Selecting and snapping still use the straight lines. View templates carry the setting with the other graphic display options. On the command line: graphicoptions {"sketchy":true,"distortion":5,"extension":1}.

Sketchy Lines: distortion 5, extension 1 (the defaults) Sketchy lines in a 3D view: distortion 8, extension 3 (the defaults in 3D)

docs.title: Plans and their cut heights
docs.text:
Views ▸ Create ▸ Plan ▸ Floor Plan opens New Plan: pick the levels and the scale, then OK. With Do not duplicate existing views on, the levels that already have a plan are left out; turn it off to make a second plan of a level.

A plan is a horizontal cut of the model at the Cut Plane of its cut heights. Walls crossing the cut plane are drawn cut, with the cut patterns of their layers' materials at Medium and Fine detail; lower walls and the floors of the level are seen from above.

To change the cut heights, select nothing (so that Properties shows the view), then Cut Heights ▸ Edit…. Each plane is measured from a level, with an offset:

Plane Level Top The plan's own level (Associated Level), the Level Above, a level by name, or Unlimited Cut Plane Always the plan's own level Bottom The plan's own level, the Level Below or a level by name View Depth As Bottom, or Unlimited Cut Heights

OK sets the four planes together, as one change. They must stay in order, from the top down (top, cut plane, bottom, view depth): otherwise the window explains what is wrong and stays open. Floors below the bottom, down to the view depth, are drawn beyond in thin lines; so are floors a little under the bottom, such as a sunken slab, even with the view depth at the bottom.

docs.title: Underlay
docs.text:
A plan can show another range of the model under it, lighter: the floor below to trace over, or the floor above to align with. In Properties (nothing selected), group Underlay:

  • Range: Base Level turns it on: pick a level (None turns it off). Range: Top Level fills in with the level above the base; pick another level above it, or Unlimited, to show more of the model.
  • Underlay Orientation: Look down shows it from above, as a plan; Look up from below, as a ceiling plan.

Only the underlay's lines are drawn, under the plan, and what the view hides stays hidden. While Select underlay elements is on (in the status bar) a click or a window selects them too, and they can be edited from here; off, a click passes through them. Project ▸ Additional settings ▸ Halftone/Underlay sets, for the whole project, the underlay's Thickness and Pattern, Apply halftone, and the Brightness of every halftone (also of Display Model ▸ Halftone).

Other properties of the views:

  • Orientation: True North turns a plan on screen so that the project's true north is up; drawing and editing work as usual.
  • View Scale ▸ Custom lets Scale Value 1: be typed.
  • Depth Clipping (plans) and Far Clipping (sections and elevations): No clip, Clip without line, Clip with line; Far Clip Offset types a section's depth.
  • View template: a template assigned to the view; while it is, the properties it includes follow it and are set in the template.
  • Show In (sections): Intersecting Views shows the section in every plan, Primary View Only only in the plans of the level it was drawn in.
  • Associated Level and Dependency are read-only.

docs.title: Light and dark background
docs.text:
Options ▸ Theme ▸ Dark (or Invert background color) turns the drawing area dark. The background changes one thing only: black lines (edges, text, patterns) are drawn light, so they stay legible (text over the rooms' colours stays dark, as on the light background); in the line styles alone (Wireframe and Lines) the paper and the black lines are inverted together, in plans, sections, elevations and 3D. In the styles that show the model's colours (Shaded, Flat Colors, Realistic, Pastel) faces, materials, fills, washes, shadows, poché, transparency and depth cueing are identical on any background, and Pastel always draws on its light paper. Options ▸ Interface size makes the whole interface bigger, from 100 % to 250 %, on top of the screen's own scale: useful on screens with many pixels. It is kept for the next start.

A plan on the dark background

docs.title: Opening a view from its symbol
docs.text:
Double-click a view's symbol to open its view: a section line or its head, an elevation symbol, a callout's boundary (a reference callout opens the view it points at), a level's line in a section or elevation (its floor plan opens), or a view placed on a sheet. The view's window becomes the active one.

Views ▸ Create ▸ Elevation ▾ ▸ Framing Elevation makes an elevation of a grid: click beside the grid, on the side to look from (before the click, a line and an arrow show the view). The elevation looks at the nearest grid, as wide as the bay between the grids that cross it and as deep as the next grid parallel to it.

The heads of sections, elevation symbols and callouts show the view's detail number over the number of the sheet it is placed on; their circles stay empty while the view is on no sheet. A new project comes with four elevations, North, South, East and West, looking at the area round the origin: move them where the building is.

docs.title: Scale, detail and crop region
docs.text:
The view control bar shows the view's View Scale and Detail (in 3D views too).

  • At a smaller scale the model is drawn smaller on paper while text, tags and symbols keep their size on paper: at 1:200 a text covers twice as much of the model as at 1:100.
  • At Coarse a cut wall is one fill; at Medium and Fine its layers show, each with its material.
The same corner at Coarse and at Fine detail

Sections cut the model the same way. Walls, floors and roofs that meet in the cut are drawn as one: a thick outline round them, a thin line only where two materials meet, none between two parts of the same material; walls attached to a roof stop under it. Each cut layer has its material's cut pattern (at Coarse, the type's Coarse Scale Fill Pattern in its Coarse Scale Fill Color, set on wall, floor and roof types, else only its outline). Furniture and plumbing fixtures are never cut: they are seen whole. A window is cut with its frame in the thick cut line and its glass in thin lines; what lies beyond the cut is drawn in thinner projection lines. Beyond the cut, and in elevations, a face in front hides what is behind it, and a window's glass is opaque: each window shows its frame and glass, not the rooms behind it.

A section: what is cut, and what is seen beyond

Crop View clips the view to its crop region, Show Crop Region draws the region; drag its edges to resize it. To type its size: Properties ▸ Size Crop ▸ Edit…, then Width and Height; the region keeps its centre.

docs.title: Hiding and isolating
docs.text:
Isolate Temporarily (the glasses on the view control bar) acts on the selected elements, in the active view only, and does not change the project:

Command Shortcut What stays visible Isolate Element HI Only the selected elements Hide Element HH Everything but the selected elements Isolate Category IC Only the categories of the selected elements Hide Category HC Everything but those categories Isolate Category: only the furniture, a coloured border

The view gets a coloured border. Each use narrows what is shown: hiding one element and then another hides both. Reset Isolate Temporarily (HR) shows everything again; Apply Hide/Isolate to View hides for good what was hidden for now.

To hide for good in the view, select the elements, then right-click ▸ Hide in view ▸ Elements or Category, or the contextual card's View ▸ Hide in View, or type EH (elements) or VH (category).

Reveal Hidden (the light bulb on the view control bar, or RH) frames the view in magenta and shows what is hidden in magenta, the rest in halftone. A hidden element can then be selected and shown again: right-click ▸ Unhide in View ▸ Elements (or Category). Click the light bulb again, or type RH, to leave.

docs.title: Visibility and Graphics
docs.text:
Views ▸ Graphics ▸ Visibility and Graphics (or VG, or Properties ▸ Visibility/graphics overrides ▸ Edit…) shows, for the active view, one row per category:

  • the check box shows or hides the category; Show model categories in this view shows or hides them all;
  • Projection lines and Cut lines: Override… sets the weight, colour and pattern;
  • Surface Patterns and Cut Patterns: the material's patterns, hidden, in another colour or replaced by another fill pattern;
  • Halftone blends the lines with the background;
  • Transparent makes the surfaces see-through in the 3D view;
  • Detail draws the category at another level than the view.
Visibility and Graphics

Clear overrides takes the selected rows back to the styles by category. Changes show at once: Apply keeps them and the window, Cancel (or the window's ×) takes back what was not applied, OK keeps them and closes.

One element can have its own graphics in a view: select it, then right-click ▸ Custom Graphics ▸ By Element… (or the contextual card's View group). View-Specific Element Graphics has Visible, Halftone, Transparent, the surface and cut patterns and the projection and cut lines. They apply only in this view, over the category's and the filters'.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Views ▸ Graphics ▸ Filters lists the project's filters: New, Duplicate, Rename, Delete. A filter has categories and up to four rules on their parameters, all of which an element must meet.

A filter: categories and rules

In Visibility and Graphics ▸ Filters, Add applies a filter to the view; its row then sets visibility, lines, Halftone and Transparent for the elements that pass it. Where filters disagree, the one higher in the list wins: Up and Down move the selected filter.

docs.title: View templates
docs.text:
Views ▸ Graphics ▸ View templates ▸ Create template from current view keeps the view's scale, detail, graphic style, cut heights and graphics as a template, by name. View templates ▸ Apply template to current view gives them to another view of the same kind: a plan (a second plan of a level too), a section or elevation, or a 3D view. A view does not follow later changes of its template until it is applied again, and the graphics of single elements are never part of a template.

A new project starts with two templates, Architectural - Plan and Architectural - Section and Elevation, applied to every new view of their kind: plans, ceiling plans, sections and elevations are drawn with lines only, the materials' cut patterns on what is cut and their surface patterns on what is seen, with no colour fills and no shadows. They carry the graphic style and the sun, so a new view keeps the scale, detail and view range it is made with; change them to change how new views start. Area plans keep their colour scheme.

View templates

docs.title: Managing views
docs.text:
Right-click a view in the Project Index:

  • Duplicate View ▸ Duplicate copies the view with its properties; Duplicate with Detailing copies its dimensions, text, tags and 2D details too. The copy opens;
  • Rename… asks for the new name (Rename View); names stay unique among views.

Views ▸ Windows ▸ Tile shows all the open views side by side, filling the drawing area: with three windows, the active one on the left at full height and two stacked on the right.

Tile: three open views

docs.title: Walls, doors and windows
docs.text: This chapter describes how walls are drawn, how they join and attach to roofs and floors, how their types and layers are set up, and how doors and windows are placed in them, flipped, moved and drawn at each level of detail.

docs.title: Drawing walls
docs.text:
Create ▸ Build ▸ Wall (or type WA) starts the wall tool, in a plan or in the 3D view. Pick the wall type in the type selector at the top of the element panel; Type Parameters changes the type, and with it every wall of that type. The contextual card Draw Wall shows the Draw group, and the options strip shows:

Option What it does Height or Depth The wall rises from the level (Height) or goes down from it (Depth) A level, or Unconnected with a value The wall reaches that level, or is that high (or deep) Level In a 3D view only: the level the walls stand on; takes the level of the surface of the first click Alignment The plane of the wall that runs along the clicks: Axis (the default), the core centre line, or one of the finish and core faces, exterior or interior Continue On, each click ends a wall and starts the next one; off, each two clicks make a wall on its own Offset The alignment line runs this far from the clicks, towards the exterior Radius With Line and Rectangle every corner between two straight walls becomes a curved wall of that radius, also where a wall ends on the free end of another (where three walls meet the corner stays sharp; so it does with a radius too large, with a message); Offset then does not apply. With Circle, the arcs and the polygons: the radius of the next one, so a click places it Join at the ends Not available yet, shown greyed: the walls drawn always join; an end's join is prevented afterwards from its control Automatic joining Not available yet, shown greyed and ticked: the walls join those they meet

Structural wall, from the Wall drop-down or the Structure tab, is the same tool: every wall drawn is Bearing (with Wall, Non-bearing) and it starts with Depth; each of the two tools remembers its own choice of Height or Depth. Structural usage is changed afterwards, in Properties.

With a placement tool active (wall, door, window, object, column, pillar) Properties shows under the type selector the properties of the next element: the values typed there go to the elements the tool places, and the rows the options bar also holds stay in step with it.

The options strip of the wall tool

In the 3D view the wall being drawn follows the cursor as a solid, with its thickness and its height up to the top level (or the height typed), on the plane of the level, with its length and angle as a temporary dimension; Shift keeps it square and Esc takes it away. Rectangle, the polygons and Pick Lines work there too: the walls of the whole shape follow the cursor, and the line of the level under the cursor is picked as in plan.

While drawing:

  • the wall's exterior is on the left of the drawing direction: drawn from left to right, the exterior face is at the top. The preview shows the exterior face thicker;
  • the space bar puts the exterior of the next wall on the other side;
  • after the first point, type a length and press Enter: the value shows in a box at the cursor, and the wall ends that far, in the direction of the cursor (grids, room separators and area outlines, sections and elevations take a typed length the same way);
  • Esc ends the chain; Esc again, or Modify, ends the tool.
Drawing a chain of walls

The Draw group picks the shape:

Shape How Line Click the start and the end of each wall Rectangle Click two opposite corners: four joined walls, with the exterior outside Inscribed Polygon Set Sides in the options strip, click the centre and a corner: the corners are on the circle Circumscribed Polygon The same, but the sides touch the circle Circle Click the centre and a point of the circle (or type the radius): two half circles of walls, with the exterior outside Start-End-Radius Arc Click the start, the end, then a point of the arc (or type the radius) Center-ends arc Click the centre, the start (the radius), then the end: at most half a turn Tangent End Arc Click the end of a wall: the arc starts there, tangent to it, and ends at the next click Fillet Arc Click two straight walls, then where the arc passes (or set Radius): the walls are trimmed and joined by a curved wall Ellipse, Partial Ellipse Elliptical walls: see below Pick Lines Click a line of the plan (a line or an edge of an element): a wall along it. Press TAB over a line to take the whole chain of lines joined to it, then click

docs.title: Curved walls
docs.text:
A curved wall is one wall along an arc: it is selected, scheduled and tagged as one, and its Length is measured along the arc. In plan, section and 3D it is drawn as an arc, made of short straight pieces no farther than 2 mm from it. Its properties add Radius (changing it keeps the ends where they are), Center X and Center Y (moving the centre keeps the radius), and Center Mark Visible, the «+» shown in plan at the centre; a curved wall has it on when it is drawn.

  • A door or a window clicked on a curved wall stands on a straight piece as wide as it, with a margin each side, so its frame stays flat; moved along the wall, it keeps its place on the arc.
  • Curved walls join each other and straight walls at their ends, as straight walls do.
  • A selected curved wall has a third blue control at the middle of its arc: drag it and the arc passes through the pointer, its ends where they are (wallarc at the command line).
  • Edit Profile is greyed on a curved wall: its contour has no plane to be drawn in.
  • In IFC a curved wall is one IfcWall made of its pieces.

docs.title: Elliptical walls
docs.text:
Ellipse (centre, major radius, minor radius) draws a ring of two half-ellipse walls with the exterior outside; Partial Ellipse (the two ends of the axis, then the shape) draws one half-ellipse wall on the side of the cursor, Space flips its exterior. Radii can be typed; two equal radii are refused (use Circle). An elliptical wall stands on its centre line: Alignment is locked, and Offset, Radius and Continue are hidden. A selected elliptical wall has the controls of an ellipse (quadrants, ends with Tab, temporary dimensions of its radii, Editing Retains Proportions); a ring's two halves change together. Its properties add Major Axis Radius, Minor Axis Radius and Center X/Y. Doors, windows, openings, joins, rooms, sections, 3D, schedules and IFC work as on curved walls. Offset, Fillet Arc and Split Element are refused; a stacked type is accepted only with every sub-wall centred.

An elliptical wall: one wall with all its layers

docs.title: The alignment and flipping
docs.text:
Select a wall: blue dots mark the ends of its alignment line, and two arrows stand on its exterior side. Clicking the arrows turns the wall over about its alignment line: the first and the last layers swap, and the doors and windows keep their orientation. Changing Alignment of a placed wall does not move it; the next flip turns it about the new plane. Changing the type of a wall, or its layers, keeps its alignment line where it was.

A selected wall: ends and flip arrows

docs.title: Attaching walls to roofs and floors
docs.text:
A wall can follow a roof or a floor instead of a fixed height.

  1. Select the walls.
  2. Selection: Walls ▸ Modify Wall ▸ Link Top/Base.
  3. In the options strip, Attach Wall: Top or Base.
  4. Click the roof or floor, in a plan, a section or the 3D view.

With Top, the walls rise or drop to the underside of the roof (following its slopes: the gable walls go up to the ridge) or of the floor above. With Base, they stand on the top face of the floor below. From then on they follow it: a steeper roof, a roof raised by its offset, a moved floor carry the walls with them.

To detach them: select the walls, Selection: Walls ▸ Modify Wall ▸ Unlink Top/Base, then click the element to detach them from, or press Detach All in the options strip. The walls keep the height they have at that moment, and can be attached again at any time. When a roof or floor with walls attached to it is deleted, the walls keep their height too.

The properties Top is Attached and Base is Attached show the state (read-only); while the top is attached, Free Height is read-only.

docs.title: Editing a wall's profile
docs.text:
A wall need not be a rectangle: its outline can be sketched in an elevation or a section parallel to it, with holes, as for a gable or a stepped wall.

  1. Select the wall and click Mode ▸ Edit Profile in its contextual card. From a plan or a view that is not parallel to the wall, Go to View lists the sections and elevations parallel to it: choose one and click Open View.
  2. Sketch mode opens with the wall's outline in magenta. Change it with Line and Rectangle (see sketch mode): pick a line and press Del, draw new ones, or a Circle. Every closed loop inside the outline is a hole through all the layers; a loop inside a hole is solid again.
  3. Click Finish Edit Mode (or Cancel Edit Mode to leave the wall as it was).

The wall takes that outline in 3D, in sections and in plan, where it is cut only where the outline reaches the cut plane; its doors and windows still cut it, also over a hole, which stays a hole. A top attached to a roof or a floor still clips it. Plan, sections, elevations and the 3D view all show one solid, cut from the same outline and holes. The layers that wrap line the holes as they line doors and windows (see Wall types and layers). A curtain wall keeps the panels and mullions inside its new outline. Mode ▸ Reset Boundary makes it a rectangle again; Ctrl+Z undoes either.

The boundary can also be edited in the 3D view: the sketch lies on the wall's plane and the view stays 3D. Only from a plan does Go to View appear, and nothing changes until a view is opened with Open View. While sketching, the wall's original outline is drawn as dashed reference lines; the sketch snaps to their ends and onto them.

docs.title: Wall joins
docs.text:
Walls whose ends meet join by themselves, and so do a wall ending on the side of another and two walls crossing each other. At Medium and Fine detail each layer is resolved against the layers of the other wall:

  • at a corner (an L), each layer meets the same layer of the other wall: the finishes wrap round the corner and the cores meet;
  • at a T, the core of the wall that ends runs through the finishes of the other wall up to its core; its own finishes stop at the face, which is open there;
  • where two walls cross (an X), a core runs through the finishes of the other wall;
  • pieces of the same material merge with no line between them; a thin line separates two different materials; the free outline is drawn thick.

At Coarse detail joined walls are one fill, with no line between them. Sections and the 3D view use the same pieces, so nothing overlaps.

docs.title: The Wall Joins tool
docs.text:
Shapes ▸ Wall Joins in the contextual card, then click the grey square that appears on a corner. The options strip offers:

  • Configuration: Butt (one wall runs through, the other stops against it), Miter (both end on the bisector) or Square off (the wall that stops ends square); Previous and Next change which wall runs through;
  • Display: Clean Join, Don't Clean Join (the walls butt, with a thick line between them) or Use View Setting.

Each change can be undone. Esc ends the tool.

The plan's property Wall Join Display (in Graphics) is the view setting: Clean all wall joins, or Clean same wall type to keep a thick line where walls of two types meet, unless their corner is set to Clean Join.

docs.title: Disallowing a join
docs.text: To keep an end of a wall from joining (an expansion gap, say), select the wall, right-click the blue dot of that end and choose Disallow Join: both walls then end square, apart. A small mark beside the end shows it; click it, or right-click the dot and choose Allow Join, to join it again.

docs.title: Wall types and layers
docs.text: Type Parameters (the tile of the tool panel while a wall is selected, the button under the type selector of Properties, or a type's menu in the Project Browser) shows the parameters of a wall type; a change applies to every wall of that type.

docs.title: Type parameters
docs.text:
The Type Parameters of a wall type, with its section

At the top are the family and the type and, for a type with layers, the three figures of Type layers: Total thickness, Resistance R and Mass per area. Below, Family with Load… (a family from the library; greyed for walls and the other system families, which are duplicated rather than loaded) and Type with the other types of the family, Duplicate… (a copy, which becomes the type of the selected walls; its name does not follow its layers) and Rename…. The parameters follow in a table Parameter · Value · Formula, in groups that open and close with a click on their title:

  • Construction: Layers with Edit…, which opens Type layers; Wrap at inserts (No, Exterior, Interior, Both); Wrap at ends (None, Exterior, Interior); Thickness (the sum of the layers in metres, read-only); Function (Exterior, Interior, Foundation, Retaining, Cavity, Core-shaft).
  • Cross-section: Thickness measured at (Core, Exterior face, Interior face).
  • Graphics: Coarse Scale Fill Pattern and Coarse Scale Fill Color (a swatch that opens the colour picker), how cut walls of the type are filled at Coarse detail.
  • Materials: Structural material, read-only: the material of the layer marked structural in Type layers, «» when none.
  • Thermal properties: Resistance R and Mass per area, read-only and computed from the layers (they show «—» while a material lacks its thermal values); Solar absorptance (0 to 1, 0.7 at first) and Roughness (from 1 · Very smooth to 5 · Very rough).
  • Identification: Keynote (typed, or … opens the project's Keynotes: codes and descriptions to add, change or delete; a row picked and OK give its code to the type), Assembly Code, Assembly Description (read-only), Model, Manufacturer, Type Comments, URL, Description, Type Mark (what a wall tag shows), Fire resistance and Cost.

    • The Formula column marks with «=» the values that can be changed. Every change applies at once and Ctrl+Z undoes it, one step each; Cancel undoes all the changes made since the dialog opened, OK keeps them, Help opens this page.

    On the right the preview draws the type as Type layers does: Section (the wall cut through, its layers side by side) or Plan (the end of the wall), with the buttons to zoom out, zoom in and fit; floors and roofs show their layers stacked; doors, windows, components and curtain walls a picture of one of them. The Preview switch in the header, beside the figures (an eye and an on/off switch), hides it and the table widens into the freed space, while the dialog keeps its size and place; switched on again it shows the preview, and the choice is kept. Floors, roofs and the other families use the same dialog, with their own parameters.

docs.title: Type layers
docs.text:
Layers ▸ Edit… opens Type layers, the same dialog for walls, floors, roofs and ceilings. At the top are the family and the type, and three figures updated at every change: Total thickness (in metres), Resistance R (m²K/W: the sum of thickness / thermal conductivity of the layers, plus 0.17 for the two surfaces) and Mass per area (kg/m²: the sum of thickness × density). R and mass show when every material has its Thermal conductivity and Density (the template's materials have them, others are completed in Materials); otherwise they show «—».

Type layers

On the left is the list of the layers, from the EXTERIOR SIDE at the top to the INTERIOR SIDE at the bottom. Each layer is a card with its number, a sample of its material (colour and cut pattern), its Function (Structure, Substrate, Thermal insulation, Air space, Finish 1, Finish 2, Membrane), its Material (a click opens Materials to choose it), its Thickness in millimetres and three toggles:

  • Wraps: the layer may wrap at openings and ends (never a layer of a wall's core);
  • Structural material: the layer's material is the type's structural material (only one, in the core);
  • Variable: the layer's thickness may vary (only one, in floors and roofs).

Two dashed lines, Core boundary · above and Core boundary · below, delimit the core. A click on a card selects it; Insert adds a layer under the selected one; Delete, Up and Down act on the selected layer and are greyed without a selection. In a wall a core boundary is also selected with a click and moved with Up and Down. A membrane layer has no thickness, and every other layer is at least 4 mm thick: other values are refused, the dialog stays open and the status line at the bottom says why.

For walls, on the row of the buttons:

  • Wrap at inserts (No, Exterior, Interior, Both): the wrapping layers outside the core on that side turn into the jambs of doors and windows; the layers behind them are pulled back;
  • at ends (None, Exterior, Interior): the same at the free ends of the walls.

On the right the preview follows every change. Section shows the wall cut through, its layers side by side and as tall as Sample height (6000 mm at first), or the floor, roof or ceiling with its layers stacked; Plan (walls only) shows the end of the wall with the layers that wrap round it. The selected layer is outlined and the core lies between two dashed lines. The buttons above the drawing zoom it out, zoom it in and fit it; the wheel, a pinch and a drag zoom and move it too, and a click on a layer selects it in the list. Below, for walls, Vertical structure (in section) gathers Modify, Merge Regions, Profiles, Assign Layers, Split Region and Reveals, not available yet (greyed).

The preview draws each layer exactly as plans and sections draw it at Medium detail: the material's cut pattern in its colour, on the view's background in Lines or over the material's shading colour in the shaded styles, following the active view's graphic style and the theme. A material changed in Materials changes the preview, the plans, the sections and the 3D view alike; the overrides of a view (Visibility/Graphics, filters, an element's overrides) change that view only, never the preview.

The Preview switch in the header, beside the figures, hides the preview and the list takes the whole width, while the dialog keeps its size and place; switched on again it shows the preview, and the choice is kept. At the bottom, OK applies all the changes in one step, which Ctrl+Z undoes; Cancel closes without changing anything; Help opens this page. In a narrow window the preview stands above the list.

Wrapping shows in every view: in plan, in the 3D view, in sections and in elevations the ticked layers line the jambs, the head and the sill of doors and windows, the sides of the holes of an edited boundary (see Editing a wall's profile) and the free ends. A door or window type overrides the wall's wrapping with its Wall Closure.

docs.title: Wall properties
docs.text:
A wall selected, with its Properties

With a wall selected, Properties shows at the top the type selector: the picture of the type, its family and its name. A click opens the list of the types grouped by family (Basic Wall, Curtain Wall), each with a small picture — a wall's layers side by side in their materials' colours, a curtain wall's grid — and the current type highlighted; typing in Search a type… keeps the types whose name contains the text, the arrows and Enter pick one. Under it Walls (1) says what is shown and Type Parameters opens the dialog described above.

The parameters come in groups that open and close with a click on their title:

  • Constraints: Alignment (Axis, Core Centerline, Finish Face: Exterior, Finish Face: Interior, Core Face: Exterior, Core Face: Interior), Base Level, Offset at Base, Base is Attached (read-only), Extend layers at base, Top Level (a level, or Unconnected), Free Height (typed only with Unconnected, greyed otherwise; at the command line it is refused, saying why, while the wall has a top level), Offset at Top (only with a level, greyed otherwise), Top is Attached (read-only), Extend layers at top, Room Bounding (untick it and the rooms around the wall ignore it) and Created from mass (read-only).
  • Structural: Role (Non-bearing, Bearing, Shear, Combined). A wall other than Non-bearing is structural, and its Rebar cover - Other faces, Rebar cover - Interior face and Rebar cover - Exterior face can be chosen (25, 35 or 40 mm); they are greyed otherwise. Estimated reinforcement volume is read-only.
  • Dimensions: Length, Thickness, Area, Volume and the ends of the wall's line.
  • Identification: Comments, Mark and Classify as (Exterior wall, Interior wall, Partition, Foundation wall; until one is chosen, after the type's function).
  • Phasing: Phase created (Existing, New construction) and Phase demolished (None, Existing, New construction). They are kept with the wall; views do not draw phases yet.

Extend layers at base and at top carry the layers outside the core below the base and above the top by that distance (a negative one shortens them), in the 3D view, in sections and in elevations; the core stays between the base and the top. At the top they extend where the top is flat, not where the wall is attached to a roof or a sloped plane.

With several walls selected the filter says Walls (n), the type selector shows their type (or «‹varies›») and each row shows the value the walls share, or «‹varies›» where they differ; a change goes to all of them in one step. Help on properties at the bottom opens this page; Apply confirms the value being typed. Every change is one step that Ctrl+Z undoes.

docs.title: Placing doors and windows
docs.text:
Create ▸ Build ▸ Door (DR) or Window (WN), in a plan, a section, an elevation or the 3D view. Pick the type, then move over a wall: the opening follows the cursor along it, and temporary dimensions measure from its centre line to the centre lines of the nearest walls across the host on each side. A door swings to the side of the wall the cursor is on; the space bar puts its hinge on the other jamb. Click to place it: the wall is cut in every view. A window takes its type's Default Sill Height.

A door: along the wall, then placed

Doors and windows get a Mark that counts up by category (1, 2, 3…), from the highest.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: Tag on Placement, on the options strip of the door and window tools, tags each opening as it is placed. The options strip then offers Horizontal or Vertical, and Leader with its length. A door's tag shows its Mark; a window's tag shows its type's Type Mark. Document ▸ Tag All tags the openings not tagged yet.

docs.title: Flipping a door or window
docs.text:
Select a door or window in a plan: arrows across the wall, on the side it opens to, turn its swing over; arrows beside it, along the wall, put its hinge on the other jamb. The context menu does the same: Flip Hand (the hinge) and Flip Facing (the swing).

A selected door and its flip arrows

docs.title: Moving a door or window to another wall
docs.text:
Select it, Selection: Doors ▸ Host ▸ Pick New Host (or Selection: Windows), then click another wall: the opening moves there, where you clicked, with its type and sill. It stays selected.

Dragging a door or window keeps it in a wall: the pointer is projected onto the wall's alignment line, so the opening slides along the wall, between its ends, with the temporary dimensions to the nearest walls, in a plan, a section, an elevation or the 3D view; there a click on a window's glass picks the window, not what is seen through it. Dropped over another wall, it moves into that wall; released over empty space, it stays at the last place on its own. The arrow keys move it along its wall the same way.

docs.title: Door and window properties
docs.text:
Instance: Level, Sill Height, Width and Height (of the type), Head Height, Comments, Mark. Changing Sill Height or Head Height moves the opening up or down; its size stays.

The properties of a door

Type: Wall Closure (By host, or a wrapping of its own), Function (Interior or Exterior), Door Material (Glass Material for windows) and Frame Material, Trim Width, Thickness (of a door's leaf, or the depth of a window's frame), Default Sill Height and Window Inset (windows: how far the frame sits from the exterior face), Trim Projection Ext and Trim Projection Int (doors), Leaves and Type Mark. A door cannot become a window by changing its type.

docs.title: How walls, doors and windows are drawn
docs.text:
The Detail of the plan decides:

Coarse Medium Fine Walls One fill (or the type's coarse pattern), joined walls merged Each layer with its material's cut pattern As Medium Windows The frame as one outline, the glass along it, the wall below seen as lines The frame cut at each jamb and at the mullion of a two-leaf window, at its inset; one line of glass; the exterior sill and the interior sill board As Medium, with double glass Doors The leaf as a line and its swing The frame at each jamb, the leaf with its thickness, its swing As Medium, with the trims out of the faces

In every case the layers end at the jambs of the opening, closed by the cut line, or wrap into them as the types ask. In sections and in 3D, doors and windows show their frame, leaves, glass and sills, in the type's materials.

docs.title: Curtain walls
docs.text:
A curtain wall is a wall of a curtain wall type, drawn with the Wall tool: pick Curtain Wall (one glass panel the length of the wall), Exterior Glazing (grid lines by the type) or Storefront (grid lines and mullions) in the type selector, then draw as for any wall, in plan or in 3D, with Continue and the Draw shapes. A basic wall changes into a curtain wall by picking a curtain wall type in the type selector; the doors and windows it hosts are deleted, because a curtain wall does not host them, and a message says so (undo brings them back).

A storefront in the south elevation

In plan each glass panel is drawn with its thickness and the mullions are cut. A type with Automatically Embed ticked (the Storefront) drawn along a wall cuts its own hole in it, in plan, sections, 3D and IFC. The wall stays one wall: beside and above the hole it goes on with its layers, its net area leaves the hole out, and moving or resizing the curtain wall takes the hole with it.

  • The type's Vertical Layout and horizontal layout (Fixed distance, Fixed number, Maximum spacing) with their spacing, and the instance's Number of Vertical Grids and Vertical Justification, place the grid lines by themselves.
  • Create ▸ Build ▸ Curtain Grid: click near the top or bottom edge for a vertical line, near a side for a horizontal one, in an elevation, a section, a plan or the 3D view (on the face under the cursor); it snaps to the middle and the thirds of the panel.
  • Create ▸ Build ▸ Mullion: Grid Line, Grid Line Segment or All Grid Lines, with the mullion type picked in the type selector; click the grid line in an elevation, a section or the 3D view.
  • Select the curtain wall, then Panel in its contextual card: pick a panel type (a Curtain Wall Door, a glazed or solid panel, or none) and click the panel to change, in an elevation, a section or the 3D view.

Panels and mullions have their own schedules, and the IFC export writes the curtain wall with its plates and members.

  • Curtain Grid ▸ Placement: All Segments (the whole line), One Segment (only across the panel clicked) or All Except Picked (click to place the line, click the segments to leave out, then click away from the line).
  • With a curtain wall selected, Add/Remove Segments: click a segment of a grid line to take it off (the two panels on either side become one, and its mullion goes) or to put it back. Panels stay rectangular: a segment that would make an L-shaped panel is refused.
  • Hover over a curtain wall and press TAB: the panel under the cursor is outlined; click to select it alone. The element panel shows its Width and Height, and the type selector changes its type.

docs.title: Grid lines and mullions
docs.text:
TAB over a curtain wall goes from the wall to the mullion under the cursor, then to its grid line, then to the panel; the status bar says what is highlighted and a click selects that alone (CTRL+click adds more of the same curtain wall). It works in plan (vertical lines and mullions), in sections, elevations and the 3D view.

  • A selected grid line: the lines of the type's layout show a pushpin and do not move; a click on the pushpin (or Tie to Type ▸ Independent in Properties) makes the line independent: it stays where it is with its mullions when the wall changes size or the type changes its layout. An independent line, or one added by hand, drags between the lines beside it (the panels follow), moves when one of its temporary dimensions is typed, and is deleted with DELETE. Its pushpin ties it to the type again.
  • A selected mullion: one per segment of a grid line. Properties shows Comments, Length (the segment, before the cut at the joints) and Mark (a mark another mullion uses is kept, with a warning). The type's mullions have a pushpin: unpinned, they take another type from the type selector or are deleted with DELETE.
  • Make Continuous and Break at Join in the contextual tab: the selected mullion runs through the joints at its ends (those crossing it stop), or stops there. The cross control on each joint swaps that joint only.
  • The curtain wall's context menu selects the curtain wall's panels or its mullions (on the vertical or horizontal grid, inner, border, all); on a panel those along its grid, on a mullion those on its grid line or across it. Properties changes their type together.
  • Placing a grid line, besides the panel's middle and thirds it snaps to the levels, grids and reference planes shown and, on the edge two curtain walls share at a corner, to the lines of the other one. With Mullion, SHIFT held places the mullion on the segment clicked only, CTRL on every segment that has none.

docs.title: Mullion and panel types
docs.text:
Besides rectangular mullions (Width on side 1 and 2, Thickness, Angle between −90° and 90°, Position), the template has a Circular Mullion (Radius) and four corner mullions for the edge where two curtain walls meet: L (two legs along the curtain walls, Leg 1 and 2), V (two legs square to the curtain walls), trapezoid (Center Width, Depth) and square (Depth 1 and 2). A corner mullion is drawn once at the corner and the panels of both curtain walls stop at its sides; at a free end it is straight. The Offset of a mullion or panel type moves it across the curtain wall, towards the outside.

The curtain wall type and the mullion type have all the identity data (keynote, manufacturer, type mark, cost…). In the curtain wall's Properties, Vertical Offset and Horizontal Offset start the type's lines that far from their justification point, and Structural Usage says how it is used.

docs.title: Stacked walls
docs.text:
A stacked wall selected, with its Properties

A stacked wall is made of sub-walls one above the other: a rendered wall over a stone plinth, for instance. Each sub-wall is a basic wall type, with its own layers and materials. The template has one, Stacked wall - Render over stone plinth (the exterior wall over a 0.9 m stone plinth): pick it in the type selector of Wall and draw it as any wall.

The stacked wall holds the line, the levels and the height; its sub-walls follow them. In plans, sections, elevations and the 3D view each sub-wall is drawn with its own type's layers, in the colours of their materials. The sub-walls join the walls they meet, each at its own height: at a corner of two stacked walls plinth meets plinth and the wall above meets the wall above, a basic wall meets each sub-wall in turn, and two stacks of different heights or thicknesses meet over each height they share; every layer closes round the corner, in plan and in 3D. The Wall Schedule lists the sub-walls, one row each. A door or window placed on a stacked wall cuts every sub-wall it passes through, its sill measured from the stacked wall's base.

A click selects the whole wall; Tab goes on to each sub-wall, from the bottom up (the status bar says «Tab · next element»). The Properties of the whole wall hold for all its sub-walls; its Alignment is the plane it is drawn on, as for any wall: the faces of the band its sub-walls fill, or the core of the variable sub-wall. Giving a basic wall a stacked type, or a stacked wall a basic one, keeps it on its alignment. Of a sub-wall only Room Bounding and Role change: the rest comes from the stacked wall and its type, and its type is changed in the stacked type. Break up into single walls, in the context menu and with the wall selected, makes each sub-wall an independent basic wall where it stands; they do not go back together (Ctrl+Z undoes it). The boundary of a stacked wall or of a sub-wall cannot be edited yet.

docs.title: The sub-walls of the type
docs.text:
The Type sub-walls of the sample stacked type

Type Parameters of a stacked wall type shows Sub-walls with Edit…, which opens Type sub-walls. At the top are the type and three figures: how many sub-walls, the sum of the fixed heights and the greatest thickness. The table lists the sub-walls from TOP to BOTTOM, numbered from the bottom: Wall Type (a basic wall type), Height in metres, Offset from the reference line (positive towards the exterior), Extends at top and Extends at base (how far the layers outside the core go beyond the sub-wall; negative, they stop short) and Flip. Exactly one sub-wall is Variable: its height is what remains of the wall's height.

Insert adds a sub-wall below the selected one, Delete removes it (never the last one; deleting the variable one makes the one above variable), Up and Down move it, Variable makes it the variable one. A positive Extends at base hooks the top of the sub-wall below («Hooked»): its layers stop where those of the one above begin. Align sub-walls to chooses the plane of each sub-wall that lies on the reference line, among those of Alignment (Axis, Finish Face: Exterior…).

On the right is the section of the type, as tall as Sample height, the reference line in blue, the exterior on the left; a click on a sub-wall selects its row. The slim Preview strip hides and shows it, and the dialog keeps its size and place. OK applies the changes in one step (Ctrl+Z undoes it); Cancel leaves the type as it was.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
Create ▸ References ▸ Level draws a level in a section or an elevation with two clicks, at the height of the first one; while drawing, a temporary dimension gives the distance to the nearest level. The options strip shows:

  • Make Plan View: on, the new level gets its floor plan; off, it is a reference level with no plan, which walls and other elements can still take as their base or top;
  • Plan View Types...: the kinds of plan the level gets (Floor Plan; ceiling plans are not available yet);
  • Offset: how far above the clicks the level goes.

docs.title: Work planes
docs.text: Every view draws and places on a work plane. A plan's work plane is its level, a 3D view's the lowest level; a section or an elevation has none until one is set. The plane is kept with the view.

docs.title: Setting the work plane
docs.text:
Create ▸ Work Plane ▸ Define opens the Work Plane dialog. Current Work Plane shows the plane the view uses now. Under Specify a new Work Plane:

Work Plane
  • Name: pick a level, a grid or a named reference plane in the list (picking one selects Name), then OK;
  • Pick a plane: after OK, click a wall (its face on the side of the cursor in a plan, the face turned to you in a section or a 3D view), a grid, a reference plane or, in a section, a level;
  • Pick a line and use the work plane it was sketched in: after OK, click a wall or a room separator: its level becomes the work plane.

A plane that does not lie in the view, such as a grid picked in a plan or a level in a section, is not set there: Go to View lists the views it lies in (the sections and elevations facing a vertical plane, the plans of a horizontal one) and the 3D views, and Open View opens the chosen one with that work plane. Undo takes a new work plane back.

docs.title: Showing the work plane
docs.text:
Create ▸ Work Plane ▸ Display draws the work plane's grid in the view, over the model, when the plane lies in the view (in a 3D view always); Show again hides it. In a section with no work plane it opens the Work Plane dialog first. Click the border of the grid to select it: the options strip shows Spacing, the distance between its lines (1 m to start with). While the grid is shown, the points of walls and other lines drawn in the plan snap to the crossings of its lines.

In a 3D view, a click where there is no element under the cursor lands on the view's work plane when one has been set for it: a component placed east of the house with the work plane set to the first floor stands on the first floor.

docs.title: Reference planes
docs.text: Create ▸ Work Plane ▸ Reference Plane (or type RP) draws a reference plane with two clicks, like a grid. Drawn in a plan it is the vertical plane through the line, shown as a green dashed line in every plan and in the sections and elevations that cross it. Drawn in a section or an elevation it is the plane through the line across the view's depth (a horizontal line makes a horizontal plane), shown in the views facing the same way. Select one to give it a Name in the element panel: a named reference plane is listed in the Work Plane dialog and its name is written at the start of its line. Reference planes are snapped to, moved, copied, rotated, mirrored and deleted like grids.

docs.title: 3D lines and 3D text
docs.text: Two elements of the model stand on a work plane: the 3D line, a line that exists in space and is seen in every view that reaches it, and the 3D text, letters cut out of the plane and extruded, for signs and lettering on walls. Both are in Model ▸ 3D elements.

docs.title: 3D lines
docs.text:
Model ▸ 3D elements ▸ 3D line (or type LM) draws on the view's work plane with the same Draw panel as detail lines (lines, rectangles, polygons, circles, arcs, fillets, splines, ellipses, Pick Lines) and the Line style list. The options strip has Placement Plane (the levels, grids and named reference planes, or Select… for the Work Plane dialog), Continue, Offset, Radius and Move With Nearby Elements; lengths and radii are typed while drawing, as for detail lines. A plane that does not lie in the view asks Go to View; an elevation or a section with no work plane opens the Work Plane dialog first. In a 3D view the line is drawn where the cursor meets the work plane.

A 3D line is seen in every plan whose view range reaches it (from the view depth up to the cut plane; in a ceiling plan from the cut plane up), in the sections and elevations whose depth holds it, in 3D views and on sheets, always in its line style. Its properties: Work Plane (read-only; once moved off it), Move With Nearby Elements (a line parallel to a wall, or concentric with a curved wall, follows it when the wall moves), Line style, Center Mark Visible for arcs and circles, Detail Line (read-only, unticked), Length and the phases. It is moved, copied, rotated, mirrored, arrayed, trimmed, split, offset and aligned like a detail line; in a section or an elevation Move and Copy also go up and down and Rotate turns it about the axis across the view.

With lines selected, Convert Lines turns 3D lines into detail lines of the active view, and detail lines into 3D lines on its work plane; a selection of both kinds asks which to convert. Edit Work Plane moves the selected lines (or texts) onto another plane, straight across onto a parallel one. In DXF and DWG a 3D line is on the model layer of its style (A-MODL-…); in IFC it is an annotation with its curve.

docs.title: 3D text
docs.text:
Set the work plane (a wall's face, for lettering on it), then Model ▸ 3D elements ▸ 3D text: write the text in Edit Text (several lines) and click OK. The outline of the letters follows the cursor on the plane; a click places them, extruded by their Depth out of the wall's face (up from a level). Edit Text (or a double click, or Text in the properties) opens the dialog again; dragging moves the text on its plane, Edit Work Plane and Pick New Host take it to another plane or wall face.

The instance has Work Plane, Text, Horizontal Align (left, centre, right), Material (the colour comes from it), Depth, Comments, Mark (one used by another text is allowed, with a warning), Subcategory and the phases; the type has the Text Font (the fonts BIMopen ships), Text Size, Bold, Italic and the identity data. The first 3D text makes the type «3D text 300 mm». A plan whose cut plane crosses the letters shows them cut; below it, in projection. Realistic views, PDF and DXF draw the text with its material; IFC exports it as a building element proxy with its solid.

docs.title: At the command line
docs.text:
The same operations, typed:

attach                      attach the selected walls to the roof over them
attach 412                  attach their top to element 412 (a roof or a floor)
attach base 398             attach their base to the floor 398
detach all                  detach them from everything
walljoin 0,0 {"kind":"Giunto d'angolo","cleanup":"Non calcolare unioni"}
walljoin 57 1 disallow      wall 57 does not join at its end
rehost 120 12,4             move door or window 120 into the wall at 12,4
door {"point":[3,0],"tag":{"vertical":true,"leader":true,"length":1}}
refplane 3,-2 3,11 Entrance axis   a reference plane in the open plan, named
workplane Entrance axis     the open view's work plane, by name
showworkplane on 0.5        show the work plane's grid, 0.5 m apart
modelline 20,0 24,0         a 3D line on the view's work plane
modeltext {"text":"CASA 12","point":[1,1],"plane":{"wall":57},"coords":"plane","depth":0.05}
convertlines                3D lines of the selection into detail lines, or the reverse

docs.title: Not available yet
docs.text: Walls along ellipses, Pick Faces, structural walls, stacked walls, wall sweeps and reveals, vertically compound layers (regions), Join Geometry, phases, and skylights in roofs.
